sections.title: Masses and Springs · Theory and Prediction
One mass, two directions

teaching.text: Every oscillation in this course starts with the same simple system, a **mass** attached to a **spring**. The mass sits at **equilibrium**, the position where all the forces on it balance and it would stay at rest if nothing disturbed it. Pulling or pushing the mass away from equilibrium stretches or compresses the spring, and the spring responds with a **restoring force** that points back toward equilibrium.
children: The farther the mass is displaced, the harder the spring pulls back.
The restoring force speeds the mass up as it heads toward equilibrium.

teaching.text: The motion does not stop at equilibrium, because the mass has **inertia**. Inertia is the tendency of a moving object to keep moving.
children: When the mass reaches equilibrium, it is moving at its fastest and carries straight past the resting point.
Now the spring is displaced on the other side, so the restoring force reverses and slows the mass down.
The mass stops at the far end, turns around and heads back, and the whole sequence repeats. That repeated back-and-forth movement is an **oscillation**.

teaching.text: The same mass and spring can oscillate in two different directions.
children: In **longitudinal motion**, the mass moves along the line of the spring. The spring gets longer and shorter.

In **transverse motion**, the mass moves across the line of the spring. Two spring segments hold the mass from either side and are already pulled tight. When the mass rises above or falls below their resting line, the segments tilt, and their pull now has a part that points back toward the line.
In the demonstration, the transverse version appears three seconds after the longitudinal one, so the two directions can be compared side by side.

teaching.text: The two directions repeat at the same **frequency**, the number of complete cycles per second. Here both run at **0.5 Hz**, one full cycle every two seconds.
children: They match because the moving mass is the same and the total restoring stiffness is the same, half from each transverse segment in the across direction.
The direction of motion changes how the restoring force is produced, but not how fast the cycle repeats.
The model has **no damping**, meaning nothing drains energy away, so the motion keeps its full size instead of fading out.

sections.title: Mass and stiffness change the rate

teaching.text: Two physical properties decide how fast a mass on a spring oscillates, how much **mass** is moving and how **stiff** the spring is. The demonstration runs three systems at the same time, in both longitudinal and transverse versions, and changes only one property in each comparison so that the cause of any change is clear.
children: The **reference system** has mass **m** and stiffness **K**, and it oscillates at **0.5 Hz**.
The **larger-mass system** has mass **4m** and the same stiffness **K**, and it oscillates at **0.25 Hz**.
The **stiffer system** has the original mass **m** and stiffness **4K**, and it oscillates at **1 Hz**.

teaching.text: **Greater mass lowers the frequency** when the stiffness stays the same.
children: A heavier mass has more inertia, so the same spring force changes its motion more slowly. It takes longer to speed up toward equilibrium, longer to slow down on the far side and longer to turn around.
Each cycle therefore stretches out in time. Making the mass four times larger cuts the frequency to half, from 0.5 Hz to 0.25 Hz.

teaching.text: **Greater stiffness raises the frequency** when the mass stays the same.
children: A stiffer spring produces a stronger restoring force for the same displacement, so it pulls the mass back toward equilibrium harder.
The mass turns around sooner at each end and completes more cycles in the same amount of time. Making the stiffness four times larger doubles the frequency, from 0.5 Hz to 1 Hz.
Mass and stiffness work in opposite directions on the rate. Mass sets how strongly the system resists changes in its motion, and stiffness sets how strongly the system is pulled back.

teaching.text: Reading the rate correctly means counting full repetitions over the same stretch of time.
children: How far the mass travels is its **amplitude**, which describes the size of the motion, not its speed of repetition. A tall swing is not necessarily a fast one.

Within each row, the longitudinal and transverse versions run at the same frequency because they share the same **effective restoring stiffness**, the restoring action in the actual direction of motion.

For transverse motion, that stiffness comes from the tension and geometry of the spring segments. Making a spring harder to stretch along its length, without changing its tension, would not automatically raise its transverse frequency.

sections.title: Two masses have two normal modes

teaching.text: Adding a second mass changes what the system can do. Two equal masses are joined in a line by **three equal springs**, one from each fixed wall to a mass and one in the middle connecting the masses. A system like this has **two normal modes**.
children: A **normal mode** is a coordinated pattern of motion in which every part of the system oscillates at the same single frequency and keeps a fixed relationship to every other part.
The number of modes matches the number of masses that can move independently in the direction being modeled.

teaching.text: In **Mode 1**, both masses move in the same direction at the same time.
children: Because they move together, the distance between them stays almost the same, and the middle spring is barely stretched or compressed.
Only the outer springs do most of the restoring work, so the restoring force is relatively weak. This is the slower mode, at **0.4 Hz** in the demonstration.

teaching.text: In **Mode 2**, the masses move in opposite directions, toward each other and then away from each other.
children: Now the middle spring is squeezed hard when they approach and stretched hard when they separate.
That extra restoring action from the middle spring makes the cycle faster. Mode 2 runs at about **1.73 times** the frequency of Mode 1. It is clearly higher, but not exactly double.

teaching.text: A normal mode belongs to the whole system, not to a single mass.
children: Both masses move in Mode 1, and both move in Mode 2. One mass does not carry the slow mode while the other carries the fast one.

The physical parts never change between the modes. What changes is the relationship between the masses, together in one case and opposed in the other, and that relationship decides how hard the middle spring works.

teaching.text: The two modes can happen at the same time on the very same masses.
children: At each mass, the motion from Mode 1 and the motion from Mode 2 simply **add**. Where both push the mass the same way, they reinforce. Where they push opposite ways, they partly or completely cancel.

This adding of patterns is called **superposition**. The bottom row of the demonstration is the exact sum of the two modes, so its motion looks irregular even though it is built from two perfectly regular patterns.
The combined motion contains both frequencies. The longitudinal and transverse chains show the same relationships, only in different directions of movement.

sections.title: Pop quiz
Three masses have three normal modes

teaching.text: With **three equal masses** connected by **four equal springs** between two fixed ends, the chain has **three normal modes**, one for each movable mass. Each mode is a different way for the same three masses to move together at a single shared frequency.
In **Mode 1**, all three masses move in the same direction at the same time.
children: The middle mass travels the farthest, while the two outer masses travel a shorter distance. Moving together does not require moving equal distances.
Because no neighbors oppose each other, the springs between the masses change length only a little. This is the lowest-frequency mode, at **0.32 Hz** in the demonstration.

teaching.text: In **Mode 2**, the two outer masses move in opposite directions while the middle mass stays perfectly still at equilibrium.
children: The middle mass stays put because the pull from its left side and the pull from its right side are always equal and opposite, so they cancel.
A place that stays still throughout a mode is called a **node**. In Mode 2, the middle mass sits on a node.
This mode runs at about **1.85 times** the lowest frequency.

teaching.text: In **Mode 3**, the two outer masses move together in one direction while the middle mass moves the opposite way.
children: Every mass now moves against its neighbor, so all of the connecting springs are strongly stretched and compressed on every cycle.
That strong restoring action makes Mode 3 the fastest pattern, at about **2.41 times** the lowest frequency.

teaching.text: The order of the modes follows how strongly neighboring masses oppose one another.
children: In Mode 1, the masses broadly move together. In Mode 2, the outer masses oppose each other while the middle is balanced. In Mode 3, the middle opposes both outer masses.
More opposition between neighbors means more stretching in the springs, a stronger restoring force and a faster cycle.

These are three arrangements of the same system, not a sequence in which another mass starts moving at each step. The colors track each individual mass, and the resting marks give the position each displacement is measured from.

teaching.text: The frequency ratios of 1, about 1.85 and about 2.41 belong to this particular chain. They are not the simple 1, 2 and 3 of a continuous string.
children: When the three modes run together, their motions add at each mass, and the bottom row is that sum.
The middle mass still moves in the combined motion, because Modes 1 and 3 both move it, even though it stays still in Mode 2. The longitudinal and transverse chains follow the same relationships.

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode

teaching.text: The **normal-mode atlas** gathers the pattern into a single grid. Each row is a chain with a different number of equal masses, from one up to six, and each column is a mode number. The rule behind the grid is simple, because each movable mass adds exactly one more **normal mode** in the direction being modeled.
children: A chain of one mass has one mode, a chain of four masses has four, and a chain of six has six.
Smaller chains leave the later columns empty, since they have no such modes. Counting every filled cell gives **21** patterns in all.
Every chain in the atlas has equal masses, one more coupling spring than masses and two fixed endpoints.

teaching.text: Within any one chain, the modes rise in a regular way.
children: **Mode 1** is always the broadest pattern, with all of the masses moving in the same direction.
Each higher mode adds another group of masses moving in the opposite direction. Mode 2 has two groups, Mode 3 has three, and so on.
More reversals across the chain mean more places where neighboring masses pull against each other. Those springs stretch more, the restoring force grows and the pattern repeats faster.

teaching.text: The fixed endpoints stay still in every mode, because they are attached to the supports.
children: Inside a chain, a mass that stays still in one particular mode is a **node** of that pattern. It does not mean the chain has stopped, since the other masses keep moving.
A higher mode does not use smaller masses or stronger replacement springs. The parts are identical within a row, and only the relationship between their movements changes.
The mode number therefore names a pattern of the whole chain, not a particular mass that happens to be moving.

teaching.text: The colors in the atlas mark mode number, so the same color across rows means the same mode number in chains of different sizes.
children: Every pattern is scaled to the same largest displayed displacement. A tall picture is not a fast picture, and frequency must be read from how often the pattern repeats.
**Amplitude** is how far the parts move, while frequency is how often the motion repeats.

The demonstration runs each mode with its own frequency, so the higher columns visibly cycle faster. Chains made of separate masses generally do not reach the exact whole-number frequency spacing of an ideal continuous string.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics

teaching.text: A **fixed–fixed string** is a continuous string held still at both ends. Because both ends cannot move, both are **nodes** in every mode. The string can only vibrate in shapes that fit a whole number of **half-waves** between those two fixed points.
children: **Mode 1** fits a single half-wave, one broad arch from end to end.
**Mode 2** fits two half-waves, with a node in the middle.
**Modes 3, 4 and 5** fit three, four and five half-waves, adding one more node each time.

teaching.text: Fitting more half-waves into the same length makes each wave shorter.
children: A wave of shorter **wavelength** traveling at the same speed along the string repeats more often, so its frequency is higher.
The five modes run at **100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 Hz**. The lowest, 100 Hz, is the **fundamental**, and the others are exact whole-number multiples of it.
Frequencies spaced this way are called **harmonics**. Here they are consecutive harmonics, including both the odd ones and the even ones.

teaching.text: One string can carry all five modes at the same time.
children: At every point along the string, the displacement from each mode adds to the others. Some contributions point the same way and reinforce, and some point opposite ways and cancel.
As the faster modes run ahead of the slower ones, the pattern of reinforcement and cancellation keeps shifting, so the combined outline of the string keeps changing shape.

A point can look nearly flat at one moment through cancellation and then move strongly a moment later. No mode has disappeared when that happens, since every component is still present and still regular.

teaching.text: The animation is slowed by a factor of **250**, so the 100 Hz mode is displayed at **0.4 Hz** and the 500 Hz mode at **2.0 Hz**.
children: All five modes are slowed by the same factor, which keeps their relative rates exactly as they are in the real string.

teaching.text: A **pickup** placed **17%** of the way along the string measures the motion at that one point.
children: Its **spectrum** plots frequency along the horizontal axis and amplitude along the vertical axis. Each of the five components produces its own peak at its own frequency.
The five peaks are equal in height because each mode’s strength was chosen to give the same contribution at this particular pickup point.

A pickup at a different spot would record different heights, since each mode moves different points by different amounts. Equal peaks at the pickup do not mean equal motion everywhere along the string.

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes

teaching.text: A **membrane** is a vibrating surface held at its outer edges. Its modes are labeled with **two numbers** instead of one, because the surface can divide in two directions. The first number counts moving regions across one direction, and the second counts regions across the other.
children: **(1,1)** has a single broad region, with the whole surface rising and falling together.
**(2,1)** splits the surface into two regions along one direction, and **(1,2)** splits it into two regions along the other.
**(2,2)** divides it into four regions, two by two.
**(3,1)** divides it into three regions along one direction.
Neighboring regions always move in opposite directions, and the lines between them are **nodes**, which stay still. All of the outer edges are fixed, so they stay still as well.

teaching.text: The five modes can all run at once on one membrane.
children: At every point, their contributions add. Some reinforce and some cancel, producing one single surface that keeps changing shape.
The combined panel is drawn with a smaller vertical scale than the single-mode panels so that it fits, which means its apparent height cannot be compared directly with theirs.

teaching.text: It is important to separate a **node** from a region that is simply passing through rest.
children: A node stays still for the entire cycle of its mode.
A moving region also crosses the flat resting surface for an instant on every cycle, on its way from up to down. That brief crossing does not make it a node.
Watching one region over time makes the difference clear. It rises, crosses rest and falls, while the region next to it does exactly the opposite.
The two numbers in a label describe how the surface is divided. They are not two separate frequencies, two different membranes or a count of how many cycles have passed.

teaching.text: A **pickup** at one marked point on the surface records the motion there, and its **spectrum** has one peak for each of the five modes.
children: The strength of each mode was chosen so that the five peaks come out equal in height at that point.

The frequencies **100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 Hz** were **assigned for the illustration**. They were chosen for teaching and are not the natural resonant frequencies of this rectangular membrane, which would not be evenly spaced.
The even spacing therefore models how separate frequencies combine on a surface. It does not establish that every membrane naturally vibrates with harmonic spacing.

sections.title: Theory makes a measurable prediction

teaching.text: The **scientific method** depends on stating very clear theories about what the world is like. In physics and in speech science, those theories usually take the form of **differential equations**.
children: A differential equation describes how the quantities in a system change, such as how displacement and velocity change from one moment to the next.
Solving the equations produces a **prediction**, a specific statement about what we should find when we actually measure the world.
If the measurement matches the prediction, the theory is supported. If it does not match, the theory has a problem.

teaching.text: The theory proposed here is that the **vocal folds are a membrane**.
children: A vibrating membrane, like the ones already modeled, produces a wave of vibration with **equidistant peaks** in its spectrum.
These evenly spaced peaks are **harmonics**, frequencies at whole-number multiples of a lowest frequency.
The equations for the vocal folds are of the same type as the spring and membrane equations, only somewhat more complicated.

teaching.text: The theory makes a clear, testable **prediction**.
children: If anyone’s **laryngeal vibration** signal is measured, its spectrum should show **equidistant harmonics**, peaks separated by equal frequency intervals.
The way to test this is an **experiment** that records real vocal-fold vibration and examines the spacing of the peaks in its spectrum.
Evenly spaced peaks would agree with the theory. A different pattern would cast doubt on treating the vocal folds as a membrane, at least for that signal.

teaching.text: The prediction is more precise than simply saying the vocal folds vibrate.
children: Many vibrating systems produce peaks that are not evenly spaced, so the spacing is what gives the prediction its force.

The membrane animation used frequencies that were assigned to be harmonic, so watching it again cannot test anything about real vocal folds. It pictures the idea, while a recording of a real voice is evidence about it.
The experiment is proposed here as the next way to find out whether the theory is true.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end

teaching.text: A **fixed–free system** is held still at one end and left free to move at the other. In the demonstration, the bottom end is fixed and the top end is free. The two ends impose two different conditions on every allowed shape.
children: The fixed end must be a **node**, a point with no movement.
The free end must be an **antinode**, the point that moves the most over a cycle.
An ideal free end of this kind can be built as a frictionless sliding endpoint that keeps the string under tension.

teaching.text: The shapes that satisfy both conditions fit odd numbers of **quarter-waves** into the length.
children: The simplest mode fits **one quarter-wave**, rising from the fixed bottom to its greatest movement at the free top.
The next modes fit **three, five and seven quarter-waves**.
These correspond to the **first, third, fifth and seventh harmonics**. The second allowed mode is therefore the third harmonic, not the second, and the third allowed mode is the fifth harmonic.

teaching.text: Only odd counts of quarter-waves work.
children: An even count would end on a node at the free end, which would violate the free-end condition.
As more quarter-waves are fitted into the same length, each wave gets shorter and repeats faster, so higher modes have higher frequencies.

teaching.text: The demonstration uses **100, 300, 500 and 700 Hz**, displayed at **0.4, 1.2, 2.0 and 2.8 Hz** after slowing everything by a factor of **250**.
children: The four modes are given equal strengths, so the spectrum measured at the free end shows four equal peaks, with frequency on the horizontal axis and amplitude on the vertical.
An antinode does not stay at its farthest position. It swings through rest and out to the other side on every cycle, while the fixed end never moves.
Counting the allowed shapes and naming their harmonic numbers answer different questions, even though both use numbers.

teaching.text: The fixed–fixed and fixed–free examples were **tuned separately** so that both have a 100 Hz fundamental.
children: If only one endpoint were changed from fixed to free, with the same length and wave speed, the fundamental would drop to half its value.
The matching labels in the two examples come from separate tuning, so they do not isolate the effect of freeing one end.

sections.title: Masses and Springs in Speech Production
Dynamic systems in economic stabilization

teaching.text: A **dynamic system** is any system whose state changes over time because its parts keep influencing one another. Masses and springs are one example, but the same kind of thinking is used far beyond physics, including in economics.
children: **Woodford’s theory** of the economy is called **Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium**, or **DSGE**.

Each part of the name describes the system. “Dynamic” means it changes over time. “Stochastic” means random shocks keep disturbing it. “General equilibrium” means many linked markets settle toward balance together.
Seen this way, an economy is a system that keeps getting pushed and keeps responding, much as a spring system does.

teaching.text: The stabilization picture follows two economic quantities over time.
children: The **black curve** tracks **unemployment**.
The **gray curve** tracks **inflation**.
In the unstabilized period, both curves rise and fall through large, sharp peaks and troughs. In the stabilized period, the swings become noticeably smaller and smoother.

teaching.text: **Stabilization** means reducing the size of those swings.
children: It does not mean freezing the economy so that nothing changes, since both curves still move.
It also does not mean turning unemployment and inflation into the same quantity, since the two curves remain separate.
The practical goal is to avoid harmful extremes, such as unemployment rising very high or inflation running out of control.

teaching.text: The connection to physical systems lies in one shared question, what produces a fluctuation and what can make it smaller.
children: In a spring system, inertia and a restoring force produce the oscillation.
In an economy, shocks and the responses of the economy’s linked parts produce the swings, and policy aims to calm them.
The curves picture the goal of smaller, smoother swings. They are an illustration of what stabilization means, not a measured test of any particular policy.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics

teaching.text: A **fixed–fixed string** is a continuous string held still at both ends. Because both ends cannot move, both are **nodes** in every mode. The string can only vibrate in shapes that fit a whole number of **half-waves** between those two fixed points.
children: **Mode 1** fits a single half-wave, one broad arch from end to end.
**Mode 2** fits two half-waves, with a node in the middle.
**Modes 3, 4 and 5** fit three, four and five half-waves, adding one more node each time.

teaching.text: Fitting more half-waves into the same length makes each wave shorter.
children: A wave of shorter **wavelength** traveling at the same speed along the string repeats more often, so its frequency is higher.
The five modes run at **100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 Hz**. The lowest, 100 Hz, is the **fundamental**, and the others are exact whole-number multiples of it.
Frequencies spaced this way are called **harmonics**. Here they are consecutive harmonics, including both the odd ones and the even ones.

teaching.text: One string can carry all five modes at the same time.
children: At every point along the string, the displacement from each mode adds to the others. Some contributions point the same way and reinforce, and some point opposite ways and cancel.
As the faster modes run ahead of the slower ones, the pattern of reinforcement and cancellation keeps shifting, so the combined outline of the string keeps changing shape.

A point can look nearly flat at one moment through cancellation and then move strongly a moment later. No mode has disappeared when that happens, since every component is still present and still regular.

teaching.text: The animation is slowed by a factor of **250**, so the 100 Hz mode is displayed at **0.4 Hz** and the 500 Hz mode at **2.0 Hz**.
children: All five modes are slowed by the same factor, which keeps their relative rates exactly as they are in the real string.

teaching.text: A **pickup** placed **17%** of the way along the string measures the motion at that one point.
children: Its **spectrum** plots frequency along the horizontal axis and amplitude along the vertical axis. Each of the five components produces its own peak at its own frequency.
The five peaks are equal in height because each mode’s strength was chosen to give the same contribution at this particular pickup point.

A pickup at a different spot would record different heights, since each mode moves different points by different amounts. Equal peaks at the pickup do not mean equal motion everywhere along the string.

sections.title: Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency

teaching.text: The **principles of mass–spring systems** collect the main ideas about oscillators into seven statements. Together they explain how a change in mass or stiffness, at a particular place, changes a particular mode.
**Principle 1** is about the whole system. **Raising the mass lowers the frequency, and raising the stiffness raises it.**
children: A heavier moving load has more inertia, so the same restoring force takes longer to turn it around.
A stiffer spring produces a stronger restoring force, so the motion reverses sooner and more cycles fit into each second.

teaching.text: **Principle 2** counts the modes. **A system with n masses has n modes of vibration**, and each mode has a higher frequency than the one before.
children: One mass gives one mode, two masses give two, and so on.

teaching.text: **Principles 3, 4 and 5** add the idea that **location matters**.
children: Added mass lowers a mode’s frequency in proportion to **how much that mass moves** in the mode, and how much it moves depends on where it sits.
Added stiffness raises a mode’s frequency in proportion to **how much that spring stretches or compresses** in the mode, which also depends on position.

**Where movement is greatest, there is no stretching, and where stretching is greatest, there is no movement.** When neighboring parts travel together, the spacing between them stays the same, so the spring between them does not stretch. When neighbors move in opposite directions, the spring between them stretches strongly, even if the point in the middle hardly moves.
In these ideal patterns, the regions of greatest movement and greatest stretching therefore alternate.

teaching.text: These principles mean the same added mass can have very different effects in different modes.
children: It matters a great deal in a mode that moves that spot strongly.
It matters very little in a mode that barely moves that spot, such as at a node.
A node of one mode is still only for that mode. The same point can move in other modes and in a mixture of modes.

teaching.text: **Principles 6 and 7** explain the harmonic patterns set by the endpoints.
children: In a **fixed–fixed system**, the harmonics are **whole-number multiples** of the base frequency, because the base shape fits a whole number of times into each higher mode.
In a **fixed–free system**, the harmonics are **odd multiples** of the base frequency, because the base shape fits an odd number of times into each higher mode.
Chains of separate masses follow the same counting rule for modes, but their frequencies are generally not spaced as exact harmonics.

sections.title: A local change affects two modes differently

teaching.text: The **pop quiz** tests the location principle on a single string. A region just to the left of the midpoint is highlighted, and the question is how adding mass or stiffness there would change **Mode 4** and **Mode 5**.
The two modes use the highlighted region in very different ways.
children: In **Mode 4**, the region moves strongly through each cycle. Neighboring points move in nearly the same way, so the string around the region barely stretches.
In **Mode 5**, the region moves very little. Its neighbors move differently from one another, so the string around the region stretches and compresses strongly.
These descriptions refer to a full cycle of each mode, not to a single frozen frame that might catch a point passing through rest.

teaching.text: **Adding mass** to the region depends on movement.
children: In Mode 4, the extra mass has to be carried through a large swing on every cycle. The heavier load is harder to turn around, so **Mode 4’s frequency goes down**.
In Mode 5, the region hardly moves, so the extra mass is barely carried anywhere. **Mode 5’s frequency is essentially unaffected.**
In the quiz’s words, increasing mass lowers frequency only if the mass is moving.

teaching.text: **Adding stiffness** to the region depends on stretching.
children: In Mode 5, the string around the region stretches strongly, so a stiffer spring there adds a lot of restoring force. **Mode 5’s frequency goes up.**
In Mode 4, the string around the region barely stretches, so extra stiffness adds little restoring force. **Mode 4’s frequency is essentially unaffected.**

teaching.text: If both mass and stiffness are increased at that spot, the two effects separate cleanly between the modes.

The stiffness increase **raises Mode 5**.

One local change therefore moves two modes in opposite directions. The location is identical in both patterns, but its role is different, mostly movement in one mode and mostly stretching in the other.

teaching.text: A **membrane** is a vibrating surface held at its outer edges. Its modes are labeled with **two numbers** instead of one, because the surface can divide in two directions. The first number counts moving regions across one direction, and the second counts regions across the other.
children: **(1,1)** has a single broad region, with the whole surface rising and falling together.
**(2,1)** splits the surface into two regions along one direction, and **(1,2)** splits it into two regions along the other.
**(2,2)** divides it into four regions, two by two.
**(3,1)** divides it into three regions along one direction.
Neighboring regions always move in opposite directions, and the lines between them are **nodes**, which stay still. All of the outer edges are fixed, so they stay still as well.

teaching.text: The five modes can all run at once on one membrane.
children: At every point, their contributions add. Some reinforce and some cancel, producing one single surface that keeps changing shape.
The combined panel is drawn with a smaller vertical scale than the single-mode panels so that it fits, which means its apparent height cannot be compared directly with theirs.

teaching.text: It is important to separate a **node** from a region that is simply passing through rest.
children: A node stays still for the entire cycle of its mode.
A moving region also crosses the flat resting surface for an instant on every cycle, on its way from up to down. That brief crossing does not make it a node.
Watching one region over time makes the difference clear. It rises, crosses rest and falls, while the region next to it does exactly the opposite.
The two numbers in a label describe how the surface is divided. They are not two separate frequencies, two different membranes or a count of how many cycles have passed.

teaching.text: A **pickup** at one marked point on the surface records the motion there, and its **spectrum** has one peak for each of the five modes.
children: The strength of each mode was chosen so that the five peaks come out equal in height at that point.

The frequencies **100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 Hz** were **assigned for the illustration**. They were chosen for teaching and are not the natural resonant frequencies of this rectangular membrane, which would not be evenly spaced.

sections.title: Theory makes a measurable prediction

teaching.text: The **scientific method** depends on stating very clear theories about what the world is like. In physics and in speech science, those theories usually take the form of **differential equations**.
children: A differential equation describes how the quantities in a system change, such as how displacement and velocity change from one moment to the next.
Solving the equations produces a **prediction**, a specific statement about what we should find when we actually measure the world.
If the measurement matches the prediction, the theory is supported. If it does not match, the theory has a problem.

teaching.text: The theory proposed here is that the **vocal folds are a membrane**.
children: A vibrating membrane, like the ones already modeled, produces a wave of vibration with **equidistant peaks** in its spectrum.
These evenly spaced peaks are **harmonics**, frequencies at whole-number multiples of a lowest frequency.
The equations for the vocal folds are of the same type as the spring and membrane equations, only somewhat more complicated.

teaching.text: The theory makes a clear, testable **prediction**.
children: If anyone’s **laryngeal vibration** signal is measured, its spectrum should show **equidistant harmonics**, peaks separated by equal frequency intervals.
The way to test this is an **experiment** that records real vocal-fold vibration and examines the spacing of the peaks in its spectrum.
Evenly spaced peaks would agree with the theory. A different pattern would cast doubt on treating the vocal folds as a membrane, at least for that signal.

teaching.text: The prediction is more precise than simply saying the vocal folds vibrate.
children: Many vibrating systems produce peaks that are not evenly spaced, so the spacing is what gives the prediction its force.

The membrane animation used frequencies that were assigned to be harmonic, so watching it again cannot test anything about real vocal folds. It pictures the idea, while a recording of a real voice is evidence about it.
The experiment is proposed here as the next way to find out whether the theory is true.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end

teaching.text: A **fixed–free system** is held still at one end and left free to move at the other. In the demonstration, the bottom end is fixed and the top end is free. The two ends impose two different conditions on every allowed shape.
children: The fixed end must be a **node**, a point with no movement.
The free end must be an **antinode**, the point that moves the most over a cycle.
An ideal free end of this kind can be built as a frictionless sliding endpoint that keeps the string under tension.

teaching.text: The shapes that satisfy both conditions fit odd numbers of **quarter-waves** into the length.
children: The simplest mode fits **one quarter-wave**, rising from the fixed bottom to its greatest movement at the free top.
The next modes fit **three, five and seven quarter-waves**.
These correspond to the **first, third, fifth and seventh harmonics**. The second allowed mode is therefore the third harmonic, not the second, and the third allowed mode is the fifth harmonic.

teaching.text: Only odd counts of quarter-waves work.
children: An even count would end on a node at the free end, which would violate the free-end condition.
As more quarter-waves are fitted into the same length, each wave gets shorter and repeats faster, so higher modes have higher frequencies.

teaching.text: The demonstration uses **100, 300, 500 and 700 Hz**, displayed at **0.4, 1.2, 2.0 and 2.8 Hz** after slowing everything by a factor of **250**.
children: The four modes are given equal strengths, so the spectrum measured at the free end shows four equal peaks, with frequency on the horizontal axis and amplitude on the vertical.
An antinode does not stay at its farthest position. It swings through rest and out to the other side on every cycle, while the fixed end never moves.
Counting the allowed shapes and naming their harmonic numbers answer different questions, even though both use numbers.

teaching.text: The fixed–fixed and fixed–free examples were **tuned separately** so that both have a 100 Hz fundamental.
children: If only one endpoint were changed from fixed to free, with the same length and wave speed, the fundamental would drop to half its value.
The matching labels in the two examples come from separate tuning, so they do not isolate the effect of freeing one end.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes

teaching.text: The air inside the vocal tract can be modeled as a chain of masses joined by springs, just like the mechanical chains.
children: Air has **inertia**. Once a parcel of air is moving, it tends to keep moving, which is the mass-like part of the model.
Air also resists being squeezed. Compressing it raises its pressure, and the higher pressure pushes back toward normal spacing. The spring-like links in the model represent that restoring effect.
The air elements move **longitudinally**, back and forth along the tube. They oscillate around their usual positions rather than flowing steadily from the glottis out through the lips.

teaching.text: The tube is treated as a **fixed–free** system.
children: The **glottis**, the opening between the vocal folds at the bottom of the tract, is the **fixed end**, where the air has little room to move back and forth.
The open **lips** are the **free end**, where the air can move most freely.

teaching.text: The two lowest patterns of this tube correspond to the first two formants of speech.
children: **Mode 1 is F1-like**. It is the lowest resonance of the tube, with all of the air moving in one broad pattern.
**Mode 2 is F2-like**. It adds one more reversal inside the tube, so some air moves one way while other air moves the opposite way.
In the ideal uniform tube, Mode 2 repeats **three times** as fast as Mode 1, because a fixed–free system has harmonics at odd multiples. Changing the shape of the tract can alter that simple ratio.

teaching.text: Each resonance pattern is a coordinated motion of the whole column of air.
children: F1 and F2 are not two separate air streams, and they are not two different places where sound comes out.
At some locations in a mode, neighboring air elements travel together while their spacing hardly changes. At other locations, the gaps between neighbors keep closing and opening.
A narrowing at one spot acts on both modes at that same physical place, but because each mode moves and compresses that spot differently, the narrowing plays a different role in each.

teaching.text: Three markers locate the constrictions of three vowels along the tube.
children: The **/a/** marker is about **one-third** of the way from the glottis.
The **/i/** marker is about **two-thirds** of the way from the glottis.
The **/u/** marker is at the **lips**.

Each marker is the same physical location in both modes. Added mass matters where a mode moves strongly, and added springiness matters where it compresses strongly, which is why one narrowing can affect F1 and F2 in different ways.

sections.title: Vowel shape locates a constriction

teaching.text: Vowels are described with two articulatory dimensions, **tongue height** and **front–back position**. Each vowel also narrows the air passage at a particular place along the path from the glottis to the lips. The chart arranges five words, dean, dune, Dan, Don and done, according to these dimensions.
The two **high** vowels sit at the top of the chart, but they narrow the tract in different places.
children: **Dean** is **high and front**. Its constriction is marked about **two-thirds** of the way from the glottis to the lips.
**Dune** is **high and back**. Its constriction is highlighted at the **lips**.
Both vowels are high, yet their tract shapes are different. Sharing a tongue height does not mean sharing a constriction location.

teaching.text: The two **low** vowels sit at the bottom of the chart.
children: **Dan** is **low and front**, and it has no numbered constriction position.
**Don** is **low and back**, with its constriction marked about **one-third** of the way from the glottis.

teaching.text: **Done** is **central** and labeled **“No constriction.”**
children: Its tract is relatively open and uniform, so it serves as the reference shape that the other vowels are compared with.

teaching.text: The labels describe related but different features of a vowel.
children: **High versus low** concerns how high the tongue is.
**Front versus back** concerns where the tongue sits along the mouth.
The **fraction** concerns distance along the air path, measured from the glottis.

Because these features are separate, one shared label such as high leaves the other features open. Dean and dune can both be high while narrowing at different places, and those places play different roles in the second resonance.

teaching.text: Locating the constriction connects articulation with acoustics.
children: A narrowing changes the local mass-like and spring-like behavior of the air at that spot.
Its effect on each formant depends on how much that mode moves the air there and how much it compresses the air there.
The articulatory description tells what changed physically, and the air-mode description explains what that change does to the sound.

They mean that the moving load at that location is greater.

In **Mode 2**, the F2-like pattern, **motion also dominates** at the lips.
Because the lips are the free end, both patterns have their greatest movement there.

Each cycle takes longer to complete.
Since both modes move strongly at the lips, both slow down, so the result is **F1 down and F2 down** compared with the uniform tube.

teaching.text: The two rows make it possible to compare the same lip location across two different resonance patterns.
children: The internal arrangements of the two modes are different, since Mode 2 has an extra reversal along the tube.
Yet both move strongly at the lips, so the extra load slows both.

The important comparison is the direction of each change relative to its own uniform reference, not whether the two formants become equal.

teaching.text: The shared direction of change follows from the role that the lip region plays in both modes.

teaching.text: The **/i/ constriction** sits near the front of the vocal tract, about **two-thirds** of the way from the glottis to the lips. This narrowing changes one physical region, but that region plays a different role in each of the two lowest modes.
In **Mode 1**, the F1-like pattern, **mass motion dominates** at the narrowing.
children: In this mode, the air at the two-thirds point moves strongly back and forth.
Narrowing the passage there adds effective moving mass, and that extra moving load is harder to reverse.
Each cycle takes longer, so **F1 goes down**.

teaching.text: In **Mode 2**, the F2-like pattern, **springiness dominates** at the same narrowing.
children: In this mode, the air at the two-thirds point is strongly compressed and expanded, while its own movement is smaller.
Narrowing the passage there strengthens the spring-like restoring response.
The air is pushed back toward its usual spacing more forcefully, the cycle speeds up, and **F2 goes up**.

teaching.text: The narrowed region does not move to a new place when the mode changes.
children: What changes is the job that the same region does within each coordinated pattern of motion.
Where neighbors move together, the extra moving load is what matters. Where neighbors keep squeezing together and spreading apart, the restoring response is what matters.
Looking at both rows keeps the narrowing from being treated as a single instruction to raise or lower every formant.

teaching.text: The result is **lower F1 and higher F2** than the uniform tube.
children: Increasing the mass-like effect and the spring-like effect at the same time does not make them cancel.
Each mode is governed by the effect that dominates at that spot in its own pattern.

One constriction can therefore push the two formants in opposite directions. The two arrows summarize two separate causes, slower movement because of added mass for F1 and faster return because of added springiness for F2.

teaching.text: The **/a/ constriction** sits farther back in the vocal tract, about **one-third** of the way from the glottis to the lips. This changes a different part of each mode than the front /i/ narrowing does, while the basic effects of mass and stiffness stay exactly the same.
In **Mode 1**, the F1-like pattern, **springiness dominates** at the narrowing.
children: In this mode, the air at the one-third point is strongly compressed and expanded.
Narrowing the passage there strengthens the restoring response, so the air is pushed back toward its usual spacing more forcefully.
The cycle speeds up, so **F1 goes up**.

teaching.text: In **Mode 2**, the F2-like pattern, **mass motion dominates** at the narrowing.
children: In this mode, the air at the one-third point moves strongly back and forth.
Narrowing the passage there adds effective moving mass, which is harder to reverse.
The cycle slows down, so **F2 goes down**.

teaching.text: The narrowing affects the same back location in both rows, but the rows describe different coordinated movements of the air.
children: A region can move very little itself while its neighbors repeatedly squeeze together and spread apart around it. That is a compression role.
A region can also move strongly while the spacing around it changes very little. That is a movement role.
At the one-third point, Mode 1 gives the region a compression role and Mode 2 gives it a movement role, which is why springiness dominates the first and moving mass dominates the second.

teaching.text: The result is **higher F1 and lower F2**, the reverse of the /i/ pattern.
children: Changing where the constriction is located changes which role matters most in each mode. It does not change what mass or stiffness means.
The full chain of reasoning runs from constriction location, to local movement or compression in each mode, to the effect on that mode’s frequency.

teaching.text: Every location in a vibrating air column can be described in two ways, by its **movement** and by its **compression**. These are related but different.
children: **Movement** is how far an air element travels back and forth.

**Compression** is how the gaps between neighboring elements change. When the gaps get smaller, the air is compressed. When they get wider, the air is in **rarefaction**, meaning it is more spread out than usual.
Elements can travel a long way together while the spacing between them hardly changes. Elsewhere, neighbors can squeeze together and spread apart strongly around a point whose own movement is small.

teaching.text: The animation separates the resonance patterns of one air column.
children: The moving **Schwa** row is the uniform-tube reference, the vowel with no constriction.
The **F1, F2 and F3** rows each show one resonance pattern of that same column of air.

sections.title: Masses and Springs in Speech Production
Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency

teaching.text: The **principles of mass–spring systems** collect the main ideas about oscillators into seven statements. Together they explain how a change in mass or stiffness, at a particular place, changes a particular mode.
**Principle 1** is about the whole system. **Raising the mass lowers the frequency, and raising the stiffness raises it.**
children: A heavier moving load has more inertia, so the same restoring force takes longer to turn it around.
A stiffer spring produces a stronger restoring force, so the motion reverses sooner and more cycles fit into each second.

teaching.text: **Principle 2** counts the modes. **A system with n masses has n modes of vibration**, and each mode has a higher frequency than the one before.
children: One mass gives one mode, two masses give two, and so on.

teaching.text: **Principles 3, 4 and 5** add the idea that **location matters**.
children: Added mass lowers a mode’s frequency in proportion to **how much that mass moves** in the mode, and how much it moves depends on where it sits.
Added stiffness raises a mode’s frequency in proportion to **how much that spring stretches or compresses** in the mode, which also depends on position.

**Where movement is greatest, there is no stretching, and where stretching is greatest, there is no movement.** When neighboring parts travel together, the spacing between them stays the same, so the spring between them does not stretch. When neighbors move in opposite directions, the spring between them stretches strongly, even if the point in the middle hardly moves.
In these ideal patterns, the regions of greatest movement and greatest stretching therefore alternate.

teaching.text: These principles mean the same added mass can have very different effects in different modes.
children: It matters a great deal in a mode that moves that spot strongly.
It matters very little in a mode that barely moves that spot, such as at a node.
A node of one mode is still only for that mode. The same point can move in other modes and in a mixture of modes.

teaching.text: **Principles 6 and 7** explain the harmonic patterns set by the endpoints.
children: In a **fixed–fixed system**, the harmonics are **whole-number multiples** of the base frequency, because the base shape fits a whole number of times into each higher mode.
In a **fixed–free system**, the harmonics are **odd multiples** of the base frequency, because the base shape fits an odd number of times into each higher mode.
Chains of separate masses follow the same counting rule for modes, but their frequencies are generally not spaced as exact harmonics.

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode

teaching.text: The **normal-mode atlas** gathers the pattern into a single grid. Each row is a chain with a different number of equal masses, from one up to six, and each column is a mode number. Smaller chains leave the later columns empty, since they have no such modes. Counting every filled cell gives **21** patterns in all.
Every chain in the atlas has equal masses, one more coupling spring than masses and two fixed endpoints.

teaching.text: Within any one chain, the modes rise in a regular way.

Each higher mode adds another group of masses moving in the opposite direction. Mode 2 has two groups, Mode 3 has three, and so on.
More reversals across the chain mean more places where neighboring masses pull against each other. Those springs stretch more, the restoring force grows and the pattern repeats faster.

teaching.text: A **fixed–fixed string** is held still at both of its ends. Because neither end can move, both ends must be **nodes** in every mode the string can take. The two halves move in opposite directions, so while the left half rises, the right half falls.

teaching.text: A **fixed–fixed string** is a continuous string held still at both ends. Because both ends cannot move, both are **nodes** in every mode. The string can only vibrate in shapes that fit a whole number of **half-waves** between those two fixed points.

As the faster modes run ahead of the slower ones, the pattern of reinforcement and cancellation keeps shifting, so the combined outline of the string keeps changing shape.

A point can look nearly flat at one moment through cancellation and then move strongly a moment later. No mode has disappeared when that happens, since every component is still present and still regular.

teaching.text: The animation is slowed by a factor of **250**, so the 100 Hz mode is displayed at **0.4 Hz** and the 500 Hz mode at **2.0 Hz**.

The five peaks are equal in height because each mode’s strength was chosen to give the same contribution at this particular pickup point.

A pickup at a different spot would record different heights, since each mode moves different points by different amounts. Equal peaks at the pickup do not mean equal motion everywhere along the string.

teaching.text: A **membrane** is a vibrating surface held at its outer edges. Its modes are labeled with **two numbers** instead of one, because the surface can divide in two directions. The first number counts moving regions across one direction, and the second counts regions across the other.

**(2,1)** splits the surface into two regions along one direction, and **(1,2)** splits it into two regions along the other.
**(2,2)** divides it into four regions, two by two.
**(3,1)** divides it into three regions along one direction.
Neighboring regions always move in opposite directions, and the lines between them are **nodes**, which stay still. All of the outer edges are fixed, so they stay still as well.

teaching.text: The five modes can all run at once on one membrane.

The combined panel is drawn with a smaller vertical scale than the single-mode panels so that it fits, which means its apparent height cannot be compared directly with theirs.

Watching one region over time makes the difference clear. It rises, crosses rest and falls, while the region next to it does exactly the opposite.

A narrowing at one spot acts on both modes at that same physical place, but because each mode moves and compresses that spot differently, the narrowing plays a different role in each.

The two **high** vowels sit at the top of the chart, but they narrow the tract in different places.

**Dune** is **high and back**. Its constriction is highlighted at the **lips**.

teaching.text: The two **low** vowels sit at the bottom of the chart.

children: The **/a/** marker is about **one-third** of the way from the glottis.
The **/i/** marker is about **two-thirds** of the way from the glottis.
The **/u/** marker is at the **lips**.

Each marker is the same physical location in both modes. Added mass matters where a mode moves strongly, and added springiness matters where it compresses strongly, which is why one narrowing can affect F1 and F2 in different ways.

sections.title: /u/ loads the moving lip end

teaching.text: The **/u/ model** adds loading at the open lips, which is the **free end** of the air column. Loading the lips means that more air has to be moved back and forth there. In the model, the elements at the lips are drawn larger to represent this greater **effective mass**.
children: The larger elements do not mean the air molecules themselves have become heavier.
They mean that the moving load at that location is greater.

teaching.text: Both of the lowest resonance patterns move strongly at the free end.
children: In **Mode 1**, the F1-like pattern, **motion dominates** at the lips.
In **Mode 2**, the F2-like pattern, **motion also dominates** at the lips.
Because the lips are the free end, both patterns have their greatest movement there.

teaching.text: Adding mass where motion dominates slows the oscillation.
children: More moving mass is harder to speed up and harder to reverse.
Each cycle takes longer to complete.
Since both modes move strongly at the lips, both slow down, so the result is **F1 down and F2 down** compared with the uniform tube.

teaching.text: The two rows make it possible to compare the same lip location across two different resonance patterns.
children: The internal arrangements of the two modes are different, since Mode 2 has an extra reversal along the tube.
Yet both move strongly at the lips, so the extra load slows both.
It does not make their shapes or frequencies identical. F1 stays the lower resonance and F2 stays the higher one.
The important comparison is the direction of each change relative to its own uniform reference, not whether the two formants become equal.

teaching.text: The shared direction of change follows from the role that the lip region plays in both modes.
children: Here, motion dominates in both modes, so added mass lowers both.
It is not a general rule that every constriction lowers every formant, since other constrictions sit where the modes behave differently.
The air keeps moving back and forth around its usual positions throughout, and the larger elements simply identify the load involved in that movement.

sections.title: /i/ has opposite effects on F1 and F2

teaching.text: The **/i/ constriction** sits near the front of the vocal tract, about **two-thirds** of the way from the glottis to the lips. This narrowing changes one physical region, but that region plays a different role in each of the two lowest modes.
In **Mode 1**, the F1-like pattern, **mass motion dominates** at the narrowing.
children: In this mode, the air at the two-thirds point moves strongly back and forth.
Narrowing the passage there adds effective moving mass, and that extra moving load is harder to reverse.
Each cycle takes longer, so **F1 goes down**.

teaching.text: In **Mode 2**, the F2-like pattern, **springiness dominates** at the same narrowing.
children: In this mode, the air at the two-thirds point is strongly compressed and expanded, while its own movement is smaller.
Narrowing the passage there strengthens the spring-like restoring response.
The air is pushed back toward its usual spacing more forcefully, the cycle speeds up, and **F2 goes up**.

teaching.text: The narrowed region does not move to a new place when the mode changes.
children: What changes is the job that the same region does within each coordinated pattern of motion.
Where neighbors move together, the extra moving load is what matters. Where neighbors keep squeezing together and spreading apart, the restoring response is what matters.
Looking at both rows keeps the narrowing from being treated as a single instruction to raise or lower every formant.

teaching.text: The result is **lower F1 and higher F2** than the uniform tube.
children: Increasing the mass-like effect and the spring-like effect at the same time does not make them cancel.
Each mode is governed by the effect that dominates at that spot in its own pattern.

One constriction can therefore push the two formants in opposite directions. The two arrows summarize two separate causes, slower movement because of added mass for F1 and faster return because of added springiness for F2.

sections.title: /a/ reverses the two effects

teaching.text: The **/a/ constriction** sits farther back in the vocal tract, about **one-third** of the way from the glottis to the lips. This changes a different part of each mode than the front /i/ narrowing does, while the basic effects of mass and stiffness stay exactly the same.
In **Mode 1**, the F1-like pattern, **springiness dominates** at the narrowing.
children: In this mode, the air at the one-third point is strongly compressed and expanded.
Narrowing the passage there strengthens the restoring response, so the air is pushed back toward its usual spacing more forcefully.
The cycle speeds up, so **F1 goes up**.

teaching.text: In **Mode 2**, the F2-like pattern, **mass motion dominates** at the narrowing.
children: In this mode, the air at the one-third point moves strongly back and forth.
Narrowing the passage there adds effective moving mass, which is harder to reverse.
The cycle slows down, so **F2 goes down**.

teaching.text: The narrowing affects the same back location in both rows, but the rows describe different coordinated movements of the air.
children: A region can move very little itself while its neighbors repeatedly squeeze together and spread apart around it. That is a compression role.
A region can also move strongly while the spacing around it changes very little. That is a movement role.
At the one-third point, Mode 1 gives the region a compression role and Mode 2 gives it a movement role, which is why springiness dominates the first and moving mass dominates the second.

teaching.text: The result is **higher F1 and lower F2**, the reverse of the /i/ pattern.
children: Changing where the constriction is located changes which role matters most in each mode. It does not change what mass or stiffness means.
The full chain of reasoning runs from constriction location, to local movement or compression in each mode, to the effect on that mode’s frequency.
The arrows describe the direction of change predicted by the model, not numerical measurements of how large each change is.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column

teaching.text: Every location in a vibrating air column can be described in two ways, by its **movement** and by its **compression**. These are related but different.
children: **Movement** is how far an air element travels back and forth.

**Compression** is how the gaps between neighboring elements change. When the gaps get smaller, the air is compressed. When they get wider, the air is in **rarefaction**, meaning it is more spread out than usual.
Elements can travel a long way together while the spacing between them hardly changes. Elsewhere, neighbors can squeeze together and spread apart strongly around a point whose own movement is small.

teaching.text: The animation separates the resonance patterns of one air column.
children: The moving **Schwa** row is the uniform-tube reference, the vowel with no constriction.
The **F1, F2 and F3** rows each show one resonance pattern of that same column of air.
The closed left end restricts movement, and the open right end allows it, making the column fixed–free.
Each higher mode fits more alternating regions of strong movement and strong compression into the same tube.

teaching.text: Compression and movement together act like a spring and a mass.
children: Compressed air pushes back toward its usual spacing, which supplies the restoring force.
Moving air has inertia, so it keeps going while that restoring force changes.
The two together keep the air oscillating around its usual positions, exactly as a mass and spring do.

teaching.text: The regions of strong movement and strong compression are found in different places.
children: A region with large movement carries a lot of moving mass, but it is not where the air is squeezed most.
A region with large spacing changes supplies strong restoring action, even though its central element does not travel far.
These observations connect the visible circles and gaps in the animation with the mass-and-spring explanation of vowels.

teaching.text: Reading the animation means following two different things.
children: Following a single element over a cycle reveals how much it moves.
Following the gaps beside it reveals how much the air is compressed.

Added mass matters most where movement is strong, and added stiffness matters most where compression is strong. These locations differ from one mode to another, and the rows are different resonances of one air column, not separate streams of air.

sections.title: The source supplies harmonics and the filter shapes their heights

teaching.text: **Source–filter theory** explains vowel sounds by separating two contributions that combine in every vowel. The **source** is the vibration of the vocal folds at the glottis, and the **filter** is the vocal tract above them, which shapes the sound the source produces. Separating them makes it possible to change one while holding the other steady.
The glottal source produces a **harmonic comb**.
children: Because the vocal folds vibrate in a repeating pattern, the source has a **fundamental frequency**, called **F0**, along with **harmonics** at every whole-number multiple of F0.
F0 sets the spacing between the lines of the comb. In the example, the harmonics are **100 Hz** apart, so they sit at 100, 200, 300 Hz and so on, extending up to **4000 Hz**.
Before the sound passes through the vocal tract, the spectrum looks like a row of evenly spaced vertical lines. In this example the lines are all the same height, which keeps the comparison simple.

teaching.text: The vocal tract filter **sculpts the heights** of those harmonics.
children: The tract has its own resonances, called **formants**. Harmonics that fall near a formant are strengthened, and harmonics that fall far from any formant are weakened.
The horizontal positions of the harmonics stay exactly where they were. Only their heights change.
The broad outline traced by the tops of the harmonics is the **spectral envelope**. The harmonics are the same, their heights differ, and the envelope is the vowel.

teaching.text: The schwa example labels four resonance regions, **F1, F2, F3 and F4**.
children: Its strongest group of harmonics sits at low frequency, around F1.

teaching.text: Reading the spectrum correctly depends on keeping its two axes separate.
children: **Frequency** runs along the horizontal axis, and **amplitude** runs up the vertical axis.
A taller line is a stronger component. It is not a higher-frequency component.
**F0** is the repetition rate of the source, while **F1** is the lowest resonance of the tract. These are different quantities that happen to share the letter F.
The vowel is made of many harmonics, not just four tones. The formants decide which of those harmonics are strong, and the values shown describe this one example rather than every speaker.

sections.title: The /i/ filter keeps F1 low and F2 high

teaching.text: The **/i/ filter** shapes the same 100 Hz harmonic comb into the spectrum of /i/. Its defining pattern is a **low F1** combined with a **high F2**.
children: The first strong group of harmonics sits near the low-frequency end of the spectrum, around F1.
The next strong group sits much farther up the frequency axis, around F2, with a weak region of low-amplitude harmonics in between.
Further strong groups appear around **F3** and **F4**, near **3000** and **3600 Hz**.

teaching.text: The source has not changed at all.
children: The harmonics stay at the same evenly spaced positions they had before the vocal tract acted on them.
Only their heights change when the tract takes the /i/ shape.
Because the source lines stay put, the effect of the filter can be seen separately from the repetition of the source.

teaching.text: The low-F1, high-F2 pattern follows from the front constriction of /i/.
children: The tongue narrows the tract about two-thirds of the way from the glottis to the lips.
At that spot, the first mode moves the air strongly, so the added mass lowers F1.
The second mode compresses the air strongly there, so the added stiffness raises F2.
The result is two formants pushed far apart, which is the signature of /i/.

teaching.text: Reading this spectrum takes two separate judgments for every line.
children: A line’s **horizontal position** gives its **frequency**.
A line’s **height** gives its **amplitude**.
A tall line near the low end of the spectrum is still low in frequency, even when a line farther up the axis is weaker. Height and position must not be confused.

teaching.text: The narrow harmonic lines act as samples of the broad formant regions.
children: Each line is a single component of the source.
The outline traced by their heights is the envelope, and that envelope is what identifies the vowel.
The values describe one schematic /i/, not an exact pattern produced identically by every speaker.

sections.title: The /a/ filter raises F1 and lowers F2

teaching.text: The **/a/ filter** reverses the pattern of /i/. Compared with /i/, it has a **higher F1** and a **lower F2**, which brings the first two resonance regions close together.
children: In the example, **F1 is at 750 Hz** and **F2 is near 1200 Hz**.
**F3** and **F4** stay higher in frequency, near **2600** and **3500 Hz**.
The source is the same 100 Hz harmonic comb. Only the shape of the tract has changed, and that change alone turns one vowel into another.

teaching.text: The filter works by changing the pattern of harmonic **strengths**, and two kinds of change have to be kept apart when reading the spectrum.
children: **Moving a formant** shifts which frequency region is favored. That is a change along the horizontal axis.
**Changing a harmonic’s amplitude** makes that line taller or shorter. That is a change along the vertical axis.
When the tract moves from /i/ to /a/, F1 moves up and F2 moves down, and the heights of the harmonics change to follow the new envelope.

teaching.text: A formant does not have to land exactly on a harmonic. It can fall **between two source harmonics**.
children: The F1 target of 750 Hz lies between the harmonics at **700 Hz** and **800 Hz**.
The harmonics near the target become stronger, because they are close to the resonance.
No new source line appears at exactly 750 Hz, because the filter can only strengthen or weaken the frequencies the source provides. It cannot create new ones.

teaching.text: This is why it is important to keep two terms separate.
children: A **formant** is a resonance region of the vocal tract, a property of the filter.
A **harmonic** is a frequency component of the repeating source, a property of the vocal folds.
The filter determines how strong each harmonic is, and the harmonics, in turn, are what reveal where the formants lie. The values in the drawing belong to this simplified comparison.

sections.title: A spectrogram places successive spectra in time

teaching.text: A **spectrum** and a **spectrogram** are two different ways of displaying the frequency content of a sound. The key difference is time.
A **spectrum** shows **one instant** of sound.
children: It describes the frequency components present during one short slice of time.
Frequency runs along the horizontal axis and amplitude along the vertical axis, so each peak gives the strength of one frequency region at that moment.
The example takes three successive spectra from the vowel **/i/** and three from the vowel **/a/**.

teaching.text: A **spectrogram** **stacks many spectra over time**. Building one from a series of spectra takes two steps.
children: The **first step** turns each spectrum on its side. The spectrum’s horizontal frequency axis becomes the spectrogram’s vertical axis, so a peak near the right side of a spectrum becomes a mark near the top of a spectrogram strip.
The strips are then placed side by side in order, so time runs from left to right. Moving to the right in a spectrogram means moving later in time, not moving to a higher frequency.

teaching.text: The **second step** turns **spectrum height into darkness**.
children: In the grayscale display, **black means high amplitude, gray means medium amplitude and white means low amplitude**.
A tall peak in the spectrum becomes a dark mark in the spectrogram, and a low dip becomes a pale one.
Vertical position now gives frequency, and darkness gives strength. A band that becomes darker is growing stronger, while a band that rises is moving to a higher frequency.

teaching.text: The transition from **/i/** to **/a/** is easy to follow in the spectrogram.
children: During the change, **F1 rises** and **F2 falls**.
The two lowest dark bands move toward each other, which matches the /a/ pattern of F1 and F2 close together.
The higher bands stay above them and change less.
In this way, the spectrogram follows the changing resonances of the vocal tract through time, which no single spectrum can capture.

sections.title: Reflection prompt
Wide harmonic spacing makes formants harder to identify

teaching.text: A practical problem arises when trying to see formants in a spectrum. Formants are properties of the vocal tract filter, but they can only be seen through the source harmonics, because the filter can only change the strength of the frequencies the source supplies. How easy it is to see a formant therefore depends on how closely spaced those harmonics are.
**Closely spaced harmonics** make formants easy to identify.
children: Imagine harmonics at **100, 200, 300, 400 Hz** and so on, with **F1 at 300 Hz** and **F2 at 2100 Hz**.
In that case, the formants structure the amplitudes of many harmonics. Several lines fall near each formant, and their heights rise toward the center of the formant and fall away on either side.
With so many samples, the shape of each formant region is easy to trace.

teaching.text: Raising **F0** spreads the harmonics apart.
children: Compare harmonics at **250, 500, 750 Hz** and so on.
Now far fewer lines fall near each formant, so the shape of each resonance is sampled only a few times.
A formant can easily fall between two harmonics, leaving no line at its center.
A single strong line may sit near a formant without marking its exact location. In this case, it becomes very hard to tell harmonics from formants.

teaching.text: Some voices make the problem much worse because their fundamental frequency is very high.
children: A **toddler’s** harmonics could be at **400, 800 Hz** and so on.
A **soprano’s** could be at **800, 1600, 2400 Hz** and so on.
Across the three spectra and their spectrograms, the picture moves from many closely spaced components to a handful of isolated traces, and the formants become increasingly hard to read.

teaching.text: It is important to see what has and has not changed.
children: The vocal tract filter can be exactly the same in all three cases. It does not lose a resonance, and it does not move one upward.
What has changed is the source. A higher-pitched source supplies fewer frequencies, and fewer frequencies give a sparser picture of the very same filter.

sections.title: Homework 4 lab reminder
Speech → Neural Networks
Five membrane modes combine into one motion

teaching.text: A **membrane** is a vibrating surface held at its outer edges. Its modes are labeled with **two numbers** instead of one, because the surface can divide in two directions. The first number counts moving regions across one direction, and the second counts regions across the other.
children: **(1,1)** has a single broad region, with the whole surface rising and falling together.
**(2,1)** splits the surface into two regions along one direction, and **(1,2)** splits it into two regions along the other.
**(2,2)** divides it into four regions, two by two.
**(3,1)** divides it into three regions along one direction.
Neighboring regions always move in opposite directions, and the lines between them are **nodes**, which stay still. All of the outer edges are fixed, so they stay still as well.

teaching.text: The five modes can all run at once on one membrane.
children: At every point, their contributions add. Some reinforce and some cancel, producing one single surface that keeps changing shape.
The combined panel is drawn with a smaller vertical scale than the single-mode panels so that it fits, which means its apparent height cannot be compared directly with theirs.

teaching.text: It is important to separate a **node** from a region that is simply passing through rest.
children: A node stays still for the entire cycle of its mode.
A moving region also crosses the flat resting surface for an instant on every cycle, on its way from up to down. That brief crossing does not make it a node.
Watching one region over time makes the difference clear. It rises, crosses rest and falls, while the region next to it does exactly the opposite.
The two numbers in a label describe how the surface is divided. They are not two separate frequencies, two different membranes or a count of how many cycles have passed.

teaching.text: A **pickup** at one marked point on the surface records the motion there, and its **spectrum** has one peak for each of the five modes.
children: The strength of each mode was chosen so that the five peaks come out equal in height at that point.

The frequencies **100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 Hz** were **assigned for the illustration**. They were chosen for teaching and are not the natural resonant frequencies of this rectangular membrane, which would not be evenly spaced.
The even spacing therefore models how separate frequencies combine on a surface. It does not establish that every membrane naturally vibrates with harmonic spacing.

sections.title: A fixed end and a free end select odd harmonics

teaching.text: A **fixed–free system** is held still at one end and left free to move at the other. In the demonstration, the bottom end is fixed and the top end is free. The two ends impose two different conditions on every allowed shape.
children: The fixed end must be a **node**, a point with no movement.
The free end must be an **antinode**, the point that moves the most over a cycle.
An ideal free end of this kind can be built as a frictionless sliding endpoint that keeps the string under tension.

teaching.text: The shapes that satisfy both conditions fit odd numbers of **quarter-waves** into the length.
children: The simplest mode fits **one quarter-wave**, rising from the fixed bottom to its greatest movement at the free top.
The next modes fit **three, five and seven quarter-waves**.
These correspond to the **first, third, fifth and seventh harmonics**. The second allowed mode is therefore the third harmonic, not the second, and the third allowed mode is the fifth harmonic.

teaching.text: Only odd counts of quarter-waves work.
children: An even count would end on a node at the free end, which would violate the free-end condition.
As more quarter-waves are fitted into the same length, each wave gets shorter and repeats faster, so higher modes have higher frequencies.

teaching.text: The demonstration uses **100, 300, 500 and 700 Hz**, displayed at **0.4, 1.2, 2.0 and 2.8 Hz** after slowing everything by a factor of **250**.
children: The four modes are given equal strengths, so the spectrum measured at the free end shows four equal peaks, with frequency on the horizontal axis and amplitude on the vertical.
An antinode does not stay at its farthest position. It swings through rest and out to the other side on every cycle, while the fixed end never moves.
Counting the allowed shapes and naming their harmonic numbers answer different questions, even though both use numbers.

teaching.text: The fixed–fixed and fixed–free examples were **tuned separately** so that both have a 100 Hz fundamental.
