children: If only one endpoint were changed from fixed to free, with the same length and wave speed, the fundamental would drop to half its value.
The matching labels in the two examples come from separate tuning, so they do not isolate the effect of freeing one end.

sections.title: Quarter-wavelength packets explain the allowed modes

teaching.text: A **quarter-wavelength** is the piece of a standing wave that connects a **node**, a point that never moves, to an **antinode**, a point of greatest movement. Quarter-waves are the building blocks of every shape on a **fixed–free string**, because that string has a node at one end and an antinode at the other.
children: The fixed bottom of the string cannot move, so it must be a node.
The free top of the string has nothing holding it, so it must be an antinode.

teaching.text: **One quarter-wave** fits exactly between those two ends.
children: The movement starts at zero at the fixed bottom and grows steadily to its largest value at the free top.
This is the simplest allowed pattern, with no still point anywhere inside the string. Its frequency is the fundamental.

teaching.text: Building the next allowed pattern requires care.
children: Adding just one more quarter-wave would carry the shape from the antinode back to a node, so the string would end at a node.
A node is the wrong condition for the free top, so that pattern is not allowed.
Adding **two** quarter-waves carries the shape through a node and back to an antinode, so the top is correct again.

teaching.text: The allowed patterns therefore fit **one, three, five and seven quarter-waves** into the same length.
children: Each step adds one more node and one more antinode inside the string.
More sections in the same length make every wave shorter.
The wave speed along the string stays the same, so shorter waves repeat faster, and each allowed pattern has a higher frequency than the one before.

teaching.text: The demonstration reveals one quarter-wave packet at a time, in every mode that contains it.
children: The four modes contain **1, 3, 5 and 7** packets, which match the odd harmonics exactly.
The numbered pieces divide the standing-wave shape into its sections. They do not move up the string in sequence.
The string itself moves back and forth, while the still points of each pattern stay fixed in place.

teaching.text: The odd frequency pattern is a direct consequence of the two endpoint conditions.
children: Only odd counts of quarter-waves can begin at a node and end at an antinode.
Even frequencies are absent because the boundaries rule them out, not because anyone chose to leave them out.

sections.title: Air moves longitudinally in vocal-tract modes

teaching.text: The air inside the vocal tract can be modeled as a chain of masses joined by springs, just like the mechanical chains.
children: Air has **inertia**. Once a parcel of air is moving, it tends to keep moving, which is the mass-like part of the model.
Air also resists being squeezed. Compressing it raises its pressure, and the higher pressure pushes back toward normal spacing. The spring-like links in the model represent that restoring effect.
The air elements move **longitudinally**, back and forth along the tube. They oscillate around their usual positions rather than flowing steadily from the glottis out through the lips.

teaching.text: The tube is treated as a **fixed–free** system.
children: The **glottis**, the opening between the vocal folds at the bottom of the tract, is the **fixed end**, where the air has little room to move back and forth.
The open **lips** are the **free end**, where the air can move most freely.

teaching.text: The two lowest patterns of this tube correspond to the first two formants of speech.
children: **Mode 1 is F1-like**. It is the lowest resonance of the tube, with all of the air moving in one broad pattern.
**Mode 2 is F2-like**. It adds one more reversal inside the tube, so some air moves one way while other air moves the opposite way.
In the ideal uniform tube, Mode 2 repeats **three times** as fast as Mode 1, because a fixed–free system has harmonics at odd multiples. Changing the shape of the tract can alter that simple ratio.

teaching.text: Each resonance pattern is a coordinated motion of the whole column of air.
children: F1 and F2 are not two separate air streams, and they are not two different places where sound comes out.
At some locations in a mode, neighboring air elements travel together while their spacing hardly changes. At other locations, the gaps between neighbors keep closing and opening.
A narrowing at one spot acts on both modes at that same physical place, but because each mode moves and compresses that spot differently, the narrowing plays a different role in each.

teaching.text: Three markers locate the constrictions of three vowels along the tube.
children: The **/a/** marker is about **one-third** of the way from the glottis.
The **/i/** marker is about **two-thirds** of the way from the glottis.
The **/u/** marker is at the **lips**.

Each marker is the same physical location in both modes. Added mass matters where a mode moves strongly, and added springiness matters where it compresses strongly, which is why one narrowing can affect F1 and F2 in different ways.

sections.title: Track air motion separately from compression

teaching.text: Every point in a vibrating air column has two separate properties.
children: **Movement** is how far an air element travels back and forth.
**Compression** is how much the spacing between neighboring elements changes.

These are not the same. Several neighboring elements can travel together over a large distance while the gaps between them stay nearly constant. In another region, the gaps can close and open strongly around a point that barely moves at all.

teaching.text: Each property has to be read in its own way from the animation.
children: To see movement, follow one circle through a complete cycle and watch how far it travels.
To see compression, compare the gaps between neighboring circles. Where the gaps shrink, the air is compressed. Where they widen, it is spread out.

teaching.text: The two properties together explain why the air oscillates.
children: Changing compression supplies a **spring-like restoring effect**. Crowded air pushes back toward its usual spacing, and thinned air is pulled back toward it.
The air’s **inertia** is the mass-like part. Once air is moving, it keeps moving while the restoring effect changes, so it overshoots and the cycle continues.

teaching.text: The ends of the tube decide where each kind of region falls.
children: The **closed end** restricts movement, so air there can hardly travel.
The **open end** permits movement, so air there travels freely.
Higher modes fit more alternating regions of movement and compression into the same tube, and each mode places those regions at different positions.

teaching.text: The moving **Schwa** reference row and the **F1, F2 and F3** rows are all resonances of one and the same air system.
children: They are not separate streams of air flowing through the tube.
A constriction at one location can strongly affect moving mass in one mode and strongly affect compression in another mode.
The effect of a constriction therefore depends on the mode being considered as well as on the place where the constriction sits.

sections.title: Compare positions within an air mode

teaching.text: This **pop quiz** labels six locations along the air column, **A, B, C, D, E and F**, and asks what each location is doing in the different modes. Answering it means reading movement and compression correctly.
children: Each marked location has to be followed through a **complete cycle**.
Watching its air element over the cycle reveals how far it moves.
Comparing its neighbors over the cycle reveals how much the spacing around it changes.
A single still frame cannot answer the question, because one frozen moment might catch a strongly moving element as it passes through rest.

teaching.text: A location with strong **movement** is where added mass matters.
children: Greater **effective mass** at that spot makes the air harder to speed up and harder to reverse.
Each cycle takes longer to complete, so the resonance tends to **fall**.

teaching.text: A location with strong **compression change** is where added stiffness matters.
children: Greater **stiffness** at that spot produces a stronger return toward the usual spacing.
When this effect dominates, the cycle becomes faster, and the resonance tends to **rise**.

teaching.text: **Modes 1, 2 and 3** arrange these regions differently along the tube.
children: In Mode 1, the regions are spread broadly, with strong movement near the open end.
In Modes 2 and 3, extra reversals add more alternating regions of movement and compression.
The same physical location can therefore be a region of strong movement in one pattern and a region of strong compression in another.

teaching.text: Predicting the effect of a local change requires identifying two things at once.
children: The **position** of the change along the tube.
The **mode** whose frequency is being considered.
Only with both can it be said whether a narrowing at that spot will mainly add moving mass or mainly add stiffness for that particular resonance.

sections.title: Vowel positions change where the tract is narrowed

teaching.text: Vowels are described with two articulatory dimensions, **tongue height** and **front–back position**. Each vowel also narrows the air passage at a particular place along the path from the glottis to the lips. The chart arranges five words, dean, dune, Dan, Don and done, according to these dimensions.
The two **high** vowels sit at the top of the chart, but they narrow the tract in different places.
children: **Dean** is **high and front**. Its constriction is marked about **two-thirds** of the way from the glottis to the lips.
**Dune** is **high and back**. Its constriction is highlighted at the **lips**.
Both vowels are high, yet their tract shapes are different. Sharing a tongue height does not mean sharing a constriction location.

teaching.text: The two **low** vowels sit at the bottom of the chart.
children: **Dan** is **low and front**, and it has no numbered constriction position.
**Don** is **low and back**, with its constriction marked about **one-third** of the way from the glottis.

teaching.text: **Done** is **central** and labeled **“No constriction.”**
children: Its tract is relatively open and uniform, so it serves as the reference shape that the other vowels are compared with.

teaching.text: The labels describe related but different features of a vowel.
children: **High versus low** concerns how high the tongue is.
**Front versus back** concerns where the tongue sits along the mouth.
The **fraction** concerns distance along the air path, measured from the glottis.

Because these features are separate, one shared label such as high leaves the other features open. Dean and dune can both be high while narrowing at different places, and those places play different roles in the second resonance.

teaching.text: Locating the constriction connects articulation with acoustics.
children: A narrowing changes the local mass-like and spring-like behavior of the air at that spot.
Its effect on each formant depends on how much that mode moves the air there and how much it compresses the air there.
The articulatory description tells what changed physically, and the air-mode description explains what that change does to the sound.

sections.title: A constriction changes inertia and restoring stiffness

teaching.text: A **constriction** narrows the air passage of the vocal tract, and that narrowing changes two physical properties of the air at the narrowed spot. Understanding both changes, and where each one matters, explains how a single constriction can move two formants in opposite directions.
The first change is in **stiffness**.
children: When air is compressed, as it is in a constriction, it resists being compressed further. Its stiffness rises.
A stiffer region pushes back harder toward its usual spacing, so the vibration returns faster.
Making a constriction at a place that experiences **lots of compression** therefore **raises the frequency** of that mode.

teaching.text: The second change is in **mass**.
children: Bunching air together makes its density larger, which increases the effective mass at that spot.
In a part of the vocal tract where the air **moves a lot**, the constriction adds moving mass.
A heavier moving load is harder to turn around, so the vibration slows and the frequency **goes down**.

teaching.text: A constriction therefore increases **both mass and stiffness** at once. That might seem to suggest that the two effects simply cancel and leave the frequency unchanged, but they do not.
children: The reason is that the parts of a vibrating medium that **move the most** alternate with the parts that **compress and expand the most**.
At a spot where a mode moves strongly, the mass effect wins. At a spot where a mode compresses strongly, the stiffness effect wins.
Each mode places these regions differently along the tract, so the same spot can be a moving region in one mode and a compressing region in another.

teaching.text: The two effects can be told apart by following the air through a full cycle.
children: Follow one air element and watch how far it travels. That travel is the movement that carries the local mass.
Compare the element with its neighbors and watch the gaps between them close and open. That change in spacing is compression, the source of the restoring force.

A label such as tongue height, or a single frozen frame of an animation, cannot supply both pieces of information. The constriction’s position says where the air’s properties changed, and the mode’s motion says how that change affects that particular resonance.

teaching.text: The same narrowing can act mainly through **mass** for one formant and mainly through **stiffness** for another.
children: One formant goes down while the other goes up.
Neither physical rule has been reversed. Mass still lowers frequency where the air moves, and stiffness still raises frequency where the air compresses.

sections.title: Use both modes to interpret the same tract location

teaching.text: **Mode 1** and **Mode 2** are two resonance patterns of one and the same air column. The column is held at the glottal end, where the air is constrained, and open at the lips, where the air can move freely. Comparing the two modes at the same locations explains how vowels shape formants.
children: Both modes move the air strongly near the open lips.
Mode 2 has one additional reversal inside the tube, so its movement and compression are arranged differently from Mode 1 along the rest of the column.

teaching.text: Three markers are placed along the tract, at the **back**, at the **front** and at the **lips**.
children: Each marker identifies the same physical place in both modes.
A narrowing at one marker changes the air at that region, and that change applies to both modes at once.
What differs is how each mode uses that region.

teaching.text: The effect of a narrowing depends on what the mode is doing at the marker.
children: Where the mode **moves the air strongly**, the narrowing’s mass-like effect is important. The extra moving load is harder to reverse, so the vibration tends to slow.
Where the mode **compresses the air strongly**, the narrowing’s spring-like effect is important. The stronger restoring force returns the air faster, so the vibration tends to speed up.
Because the two modes can be doing different things at the same marker, one narrowing can move **F1** and **F2** in different directions.

teaching.text: The two modes have a simple fixed relationship only in an ideal case.
children: In the uniform reference tube, with no constriction, Mode 2 runs at **three times** the frequency of Mode 1, the odd-multiple pattern of a fixed–free system.
Once the tract changes shape, the formants move and that simple ratio no longer holds.

teaching.text: It is important to keep formants and harmonics apart.
children: **Formants** are resonances of the vocal tract. They change whenever the tract changes shape.
**Harmonics** are components of the source. Their spacing comes from how fast the vocal folds repeat, and it changes with pitch, not with vowel shape.

sections.title: Lip loading lowers both F1 and F2 in the /u/ model

teaching.text: The **/u/ model** adds loading at the open lips, which is the **free end** of the air column. Loading the lips means that more air has to be moved back and forth there. In the model, the elements at the lips are drawn larger to represent this greater **effective mass**.
children: The larger elements do not mean the air molecules themselves have become heavier.
They mean that the moving load at that location is greater.

teaching.text: Both of the lowest resonance patterns move strongly at the free end.
children: In **Mode 1**, the F1-like pattern, **motion dominates** at the lips.
In **Mode 2**, the F2-like pattern, **motion also dominates** at the lips.
Because the lips are the free end, both patterns have their greatest movement there.

teaching.text: Adding mass where motion dominates slows the oscillation.
children: More moving mass is harder to speed up and harder to reverse.
Each cycle takes longer to complete.
Since both modes move strongly at the lips, both slow down, so the result is **F1 down and F2 down** compared with the uniform tube.

teaching.text: The two rows make it possible to compare the same lip location across two different resonance patterns.
children: The internal arrangements of the two modes are different, since Mode 2 has an extra reversal along the tube.
Yet both move strongly at the lips, so the extra load slows both.
It does not make their shapes or frequencies identical. F1 stays the lower resonance and F2 stays the higher one.
The important comparison is the direction of each change relative to its own uniform reference, not whether the two formants become equal.

teaching.text: The shared direction of change follows from the role that the lip region plays in both modes.
children: Here, motion dominates in both modes, so added mass lowers both.
It is not a general rule that every constriction lowers every formant, since other constrictions sit where the modes behave differently.
The air keeps moving back and forth around its usual positions throughout, and the larger elements simply identify the load involved in that movement.

sections.title: A front constriction separates the effects on F1 and F2

teaching.text: The **/i/ constriction** sits near the front of the vocal tract, about **two-thirds** of the way from the glottis to the lips. This narrowing changes one physical region, but that region plays a different role in each of the two lowest modes.
In **Mode 1**, the F1-like pattern, **mass motion dominates** at the narrowing.
children: In this mode, the air at the two-thirds point moves strongly back and forth.
Narrowing the passage there adds effective moving mass, and that extra moving load is harder to reverse.
Each cycle takes longer, so **F1 goes down**.

teaching.text: In **Mode 2**, the F2-like pattern, **springiness dominates** at the same narrowing.
children: In this mode, the air at the two-thirds point is strongly compressed and expanded, while its own movement is smaller.
Narrowing the passage there strengthens the spring-like restoring response.
The air is pushed back toward its usual spacing more forcefully, the cycle speeds up, and **F2 goes up**.

teaching.text: The narrowed region does not move to a new place when the mode changes.
children: What changes is the job that the same region does within each coordinated pattern of motion.
Where neighbors move together, the extra moving load is what matters. Where neighbors keep squeezing together and spreading apart, the restoring response is what matters.
Looking at both rows keeps the narrowing from being treated as a single instruction to raise or lower every formant.

teaching.text: The result is **lower F1 and higher F2** than the uniform tube.
children: Increasing the mass-like effect and the spring-like effect at the same time does not make them cancel.
Each mode is governed by the effect that dominates at that spot in its own pattern.

One constriction can therefore push the two formants in opposite directions. The two arrows summarize two separate causes, slower movement because of added mass for F1 and faster return because of added springiness for F2.

sections.title: A back constriction reverses the F1 and F2 pattern

teaching.text: The **/a/ constriction** sits farther back in the vocal tract, about **one-third** of the way from the glottis to the lips. This changes a different part of each mode than the front /i/ narrowing does, while the basic effects of mass and stiffness stay exactly the same.
In **Mode 1**, the F1-like pattern, **springiness dominates** at the narrowing.
children: In this mode, the air at the one-third point is strongly compressed and expanded.
Narrowing the passage there strengthens the restoring response, so the air is pushed back toward its usual spacing more forcefully.
The cycle speeds up, so **F1 goes up**.

teaching.text: In **Mode 2**, the F2-like pattern, **mass motion dominates** at the narrowing.
children: In this mode, the air at the one-third point moves strongly back and forth.
Narrowing the passage there adds effective moving mass, which is harder to reverse.
The cycle slows down, so **F2 goes down**.

teaching.text: The narrowing affects the same back location in both rows, but the rows describe different coordinated movements of the air.
children: A region can move very little itself while its neighbors repeatedly squeeze together and spread apart around it. That is a compression role.
A region can also move strongly while the spacing around it changes very little. That is a movement role.
At the one-third point, Mode 1 gives the region a compression role and Mode 2 gives it a movement role, which is why springiness dominates the first and moving mass dominates the second.

teaching.text: The result is **higher F1 and lower F2**, the reverse of the /i/ pattern.
children: Changing where the constriction is located changes which role matters most in each mode. It does not change what mass or stiffness means.
The full chain of reasoning runs from constriction location, to local movement or compression in each mode, to the effect on that mode’s frequency.
The arrows describe the direction of change predicted by the model, not numerical measurements of how large each change is.

sections.title: Air motion and compression in the vocal-tract modes

teaching.text: Every location in a vibrating air column can be described in two ways, by its **movement** and by its **compression**. These are related but different.
children: **Movement** is how far an air element travels back and forth.

**Compression** is how the gaps between neighboring elements change. When the gaps get smaller, the air is compressed. When they get wider, the air is in **rarefaction**, meaning it is more spread out than usual.
Elements can travel a long way together while the spacing between them hardly changes. Elsewhere, neighbors can squeeze together and spread apart strongly around a point whose own movement is small.

teaching.text: The animation separates the resonance patterns of one air column.
children: The moving **Schwa** row is the uniform-tube reference, the vowel with no constriction.
The **F1, F2 and F3** rows each show one resonance pattern of that same column of air.
The closed left end restricts movement, and the open right end allows it, making the column fixed–free.
Each higher mode fits more alternating regions of strong movement and strong compression into the same tube.

teaching.text: Compression and movement together act like a spring and a mass.
children: Compressed air pushes back toward its usual spacing, which supplies the restoring force.
Moving air has inertia, so it keeps going while that restoring force changes.
The two together keep the air oscillating around its usual positions, exactly as a mass and spring do.

teaching.text: The regions of strong movement and strong compression are found in different places.
children: A region with large movement carries a lot of moving mass, but it is not where the air is squeezed most.
A region with large spacing changes supplies strong restoring action, even though its central element does not travel far.
These observations connect the visible circles and gaps in the animation with the mass-and-spring explanation of vowels.

teaching.text: Reading the animation means following two different things.
children: Following a single element over a cycle reveals how much it moves.
Following the gaps beside it reveals how much the air is compressed.

Added mass matters most where movement is strong, and added stiffness matters most where compression is strong. These locations differ from one mode to another, and the rows are different resonances of one air column, not separate streams of air.

sections.title: The vocal-fold source sets harmonic spacing

teaching.text: The vocal folds supply the voiced **source** of speech. Their repetition rate is **F0**, the fundamental frequency, and F0 sets the spacing between the harmonic lines in the source spectrum.
The top row returns to the **fixed–fixed membrane**, with its five modes and their sum.
children: A pickup point records the combined motion of all five modes, which gives a spectrum with evenly spaced peaks.
These membrane frequencies were assigned for the illustration. They model harmonic spacing without claiming that every natural membrane vibrates at harmonic frequencies.

teaching.text: The bottom row presents **three source spectra**, all before the vocal tract filter acts, in the same **0 to 4000 Hz** window.
children: With **F0 at 100 Hz**, the harmonic lines are packed closely, with many lines in the window.
With **F0 at 250 Hz**, the harmonics fall at **250, 500, 750** and onward. These come from **tighter, lighter vocal folds**.
With **F0 at 350 Hz**, the harmonics fall at **350, 700, 1050** and onward. These come from **very tight and light vocal folds**.

teaching.text: In the same window, **lower F0 gives denser harmonic sampling**, and **higher F0 gives sparser sampling**.
children: The comparison links heavier, looser vocal folds with slower repetition, and lighter, tighter folds with faster repetition.
This follows the same mass–spring logic as every other oscillator. Mass resists changes in movement and slows the cycle, while tension supplies the restoring force and speeds it up.

teaching.text: A voiced vowel contains **many frequencies** at once, not just one.
children: The repetition of the source determines which harmonic frequencies are available.
The vocal tract then strengthens some regions of the spectrum and weakens others.

Changing pitch changes the spacing of the source harmonics, while changing vowel shape changes the tract’s favored regions. These are two distinct contributions to the same sound, and they can be changed independently.

sections.title: The vocal-tract filter favors nearby harmonics

teaching.text: The **filter** in source–filter theory is the vocal tract, modeled as a **fixed–free** tube with one end closed and one end open. It selects **formants**, and its core rule can be stated in two sentences.
children: **A formant encourages the closest harmonics to be audible.**
**Harmonics far from that formant are muted.**
The voiced source supplies the harmonics, and the filter chooses which of them survive. In this sense, the vowel shape is the filter.

teaching.text: A formant acts like a pulse of emphasis in the spectrum.
children: Harmonics that fall near the center of a formant are strengthened.
Harmonics that fall far from every formant are weakened.
The result is a spectrum in which only certain regions stand out.

teaching.text: Each vowel shape places its formants at different frequencies.
children: **Schwa**, the neutral vowel, has well-separated first and second resonances, near **500** and **1500 Hz**.
**/u/** places both lower, near **300** and **1000 Hz**, and also marks a third formant near **2000 Hz**.
The front vowel **/i/ or /ɪ/** has a low F1 near **300 Hz** and a much higher F2 near **2200 Hz**, so its first two formants are far apart.
**/a/** places its first two targets close together, at **800** and **900 Hz**.
These values belong to this particular illustration.

teaching.text: Changing the position of the tongue and lips changes the tract’s shape, and that moves these favored frequency regions.
children: Each formant target lifts the harmonics that sit nearest to it.
Harmonics between targets stay weak, which creates the valleys between formant peaks.

teaching.text: It is important to separate the formant targets from the harmonic lines.
children: A **formant target** identifies a resonance of the tract, a property of the filter.
A **harmonic line** identifies a component of the source, a property of the vocal folds.

A target can lie between two source lines and still strengthen the harmonics on either side of it. Filtering changes their heights without creating a new component at each target, so source spacing and the filter’s pattern are different properties.

sections.title: One filter can look different at different pitches

teaching.text: This grid compares **the same vowel filter at different pitches**. Source rows run across, and vowel filter columns run down, so every cell combines one source with one filter. **Dashed red ticks** mark the formant targets of each filter, and **colored stems** mark the actual harmonics after filtering.
Each row holds the source fixed.
children: The top row comes from **heavy, loose** vocal folds, with the lowest F0 and closely spaced harmonics.
The middle row comes from **lighter, tighter** folds, with **F0 at 250 Hz**.
The bottom row comes from the **lightest, tightest** folds, with **F0 at 350 Hz** and widely spaced harmonics.

teaching.text: Each column holds the vowel filter fixed.
children: Moving down a column changes only F0, so the formant ticks stay in exactly the same places while the harmonic stems spread apart.
Moving across a row changes only the vowel filter, so the harmonic stems stay put while the formant ticks move.
This arrangement separates the effects of the source from the effects of tract shape.

teaching.text: **Dense harmonics trace the formant shape well.**
children: With a low F0, many harmonics fall near each resonance.
Their heights rise toward each formant and fall away from it, drawing the filter’s **envelope**, the smooth outline of favored strengths.
More harmonics in the window give a smoother, easier-to-read shaped spectrum.

teaching.text: **Sparse harmonics can miss a formant or make it look ambiguous.**
children: With a high F0, the gaps between stems widen, so each formant is sampled by fewer harmonics.
A strong stem may sit beside a formant target instead of directly on it, even though the target has not moved.

The two close /a/ targets can then look like one grouped region instead of two separate peaks. Closer harmonics give more information, but they still do not guarantee two clearly separate peaks for formants that are very near each other.

teaching.text: Difficulty reading a formant does not mean that the resonance has disappeared.
children: The ticks stay in the same place within every column.
A line’s horizontal position gives its frequency, and its height gives its strength.
When the targets are unchanged but the stems have spread apart, the change has come from the source, and the filter has stayed the same.

sections.title: Map spectra into a spectrogram

teaching.text: A **spectrum** shows the sound at **one instant**, and a **spectrogram** **stacks many spectra over time**. Converting from one display to the other takes two steps.
In a **spectrum**, frequency runs along the horizontal axis and peak height gives amplitude.
children: Each spectrum describes one short slice of sound.
The sequence contains three slices of **/i/** followed by three slices of **/a/**.

teaching.text: The **first step** maps the spectrum’s frequency axis onto the spectrogram’s **vertical axis**.
children: Each spectrum is turned on its side, so a peak at the right of a spectrum, a high frequency, becomes a mark near the top of the spectrogram.
The slices are then placed side by side from left to right in time order.
In the finished spectrogram, time runs left to right and frequency runs from bottom to top.

teaching.text: The **second step** turns **spectrum height into darkness**.
children: **Black** means high amplitude, **gray** means medium and **white** means low.
A tall peak becomes a dark mark, and a low dip becomes a pale one.
Two kinds of change can now be read separately. A **rising** band is moving to a higher frequency. A **darkening** band is becoming stronger at the frequency where it already sits.

teaching.text: The horizontal axis means something different in each display.
children: Moving to the right in a **spectrum** means moving to a higher frequency.
Moving to the right in a **spectrogram** means moving to a later time.

teaching.text: During the **/i/ to /a/** transition, the first strong band **rises** and the second strong band **falls**, bringing them toward each other.
children: One upper band also moves down, while a fainter band stays in the high-frequency region.
Connecting neighboring slices traces the changing resonance pattern of the vocal tract.
Position and darkness carry different information about that change, position giving frequency and darkness giving strength.

sections.title: Reflection prompt
Speech-complexity experiment prompt
Use formants as input to vowel recognition

teaching.text: Speech science leads **back to AI**. The plan is to build a **neural network**, or **NN**, that is trained on students’ own **formants** and decides which vowel is being spoken. This connects everything about how the vocal tract shapes vowels to a computational system that learns to recognize them.
The network’s inputs are **F1** and **F2**.
children: F1 and F2 are the first two resonance regions emphasized by the vocal tract, the formants that the mass–spring model of the tract explains.
They provide a compact pair of measurements for each vowel.

The network does not need every individual point in the waveform. Two numbers already carry much of what distinguishes one vowel from another, because tongue position and lip shape move these two formants in characteristic ways.

teaching.text: The **input** and the **output** are different kinds of information.
children: The input is a pair of measurements of the sound, the two formant frequencies.
The intended output distinguishes between candidate vowel categories, picking out which vowel was spoken.
Knowing the formant pair supplies evidence about the sound. Knowing the true label tells which category that example actually belongs to.
Recognition means learning to relate the measured pattern to the correct category.

teaching.text: The proposed exercise links the physical explanation of speech with AI.
children: The mass–spring account explains where F1 and F2 come from and why different vowels have different values.
The network learns the relationship between those two numbers and the vowel categories, using students’ formant measurements as training data.
At this stage, the inputs and the task are set. Showing that the network actually recognizes vowels well would require the results of training and testing it on real examples.

sections.title: A fully connected linear vowel network

teaching.text: The vowel network is a **purely linear** feed-forward network. Its structure runs from **2 inputs**, through **hidden layers of 3, 2 and 4 neurons**, to **5 outputs**, one per word, and it uses **no activation functions**.
The two inputs are **F1** and **F2**.
children: Their order matters, because each input position stands for one particular formant.
Swapping them would change their meaning for the network.

teaching.text: Every layer is **fully connected**.
children: Each receiving neuron connects to every neuron in the layer before it.
Each connection has its own **weight**, a number that sets how strongly that incoming value counts.
A receiving neuron multiplies each incoming value by the weight on its connection and then adds all of those products together. That sum is the neuron’s value.

teaching.text: The **hidden layers** hold intermediate combinations of the inputs.
children: The first hidden layer has **three** neurons, the second has **two** and the third has **four**.
Each hidden value is a new weighted combination of the values before it. Hidden values are not new measured formants, and they are not finished vowel categories.
Because each neuron has its own weights, different neurons combine the same inputs in different ways.

teaching.text: The **five outputs** correspond, from top to bottom, to **/done/, /dune/, /dean/, /Don/** and **/Dan/**.
children: Keeping that order fixed preserves the meaning of each output value, so the first output always refers to /done/.

teaching.text: **Purely linear** means that no activation function appears between the layers.
children: Each layer passes its weighted sums directly to the next layer.
The whole network is therefore a chain of weighted sums from input to output.
Passing these sums forward describes the computation, but it does not by itself guarantee that the five final values behave like probabilities. A separate step would be needed for that.

sections.title: Random weights assign signed contributions to connections

teaching.text: An example input enters the network with **F1 = 320** and **F2 = 2000**. Before training begins, **every edge gets a random weight**.
The input and the weights play completely different roles.
children: The inputs are **measurements** of the sound, the two formant frequencies of one vowel example.
The **weights** are the network’s **settings**. They determine how the network combines the measurements as they pass from layer to layer.
Changing the weights can change every internal result, even when the input pair stays exactly the same.

teaching.text: Each connection supplies one weight, and each neuron combines its inputs the same way.
children: A neuron multiplies each incoming value by its weight and adds the products.
A neuron in the first hidden layer receives both F1 and F2, so it has two incoming weights, one for each formant.
The three neurons in that layer each have their own pair of weights, so they form three different combinations of the same two inputs.

teaching.text: **Before training, every weight is a random number between −1 and 1.**
children: The heading says **blue for positive** weights and **orange for negative** weights, though the negative edges appear green in the rendered figure. The safest guide is the written number on each edge, whose sign gives the direction of the contribution and whose size gives its strength.

A positive weight passes its input along with the same sign, and a negative weight flips it. Positive and negative contributions can therefore reinforce or oppose one another when a neuron adds them up.

teaching.text: The displayed weights are **random starting values**. They contain no learned knowledge about vowels.
children: A **forward pass** processes an example using whatever weights the network currently has.
**Learning** is the separate process that changes those weights so that the outputs become more accurate.
Naming the outputs /done/, /dune/ and so on does not mean the untrained network already recognizes those words correctly.

sections.title: Forward flow and an illustrative output distribution

teaching.text: In the **forward flow**, the input flows forward **layer by layer** through the network. At the output, the network produces **a distribution over the five words**, a set of numbers that says how much support each word gets.
The animation carries the input forward step by step.
children: Dots carry the formant values along the connections from the inputs to the first hidden layer.
Each layer combines the values from the previous layer using its current weights and passes the results on.
The process repeats until the output layer is reached. This is the **forward pass**. Learning would require an additional process that changes the weights.

teaching.text: The illustrated output distribution assigns a probability to each word.
children: **/done/** receives **0.5**.
**/Dan/** receives **0.2**.
**/dune/**, **/dean/** and **/Don/** receive **0.1** each.
/done/ is therefore the favored prediction, while the other words keep some smaller amount of support.

teaching.text: A valid probability distribution has two properties.
children: Every value lies between zero and one.
All of the values add up to exactly one.
These five values, 0.5, 0.1, 0.1, 0.1 and 0.2, satisfy both conditions.

teaching.text: The bars illustrate the intended kind of output rather than a computed result.
children: The purely linear network contains no step that forces its outputs to become a probability distribution.
The bars therefore picture what the network is meant to produce, not a verified result of the particular random weights shown.

teaching.text: The **predicted category** and the **true category** are different things.
children: The predicted category is the word the model favors, here /done/.
The true category is the example’s actual label, the vowel that was really spoken.
Judging whether a prediction is correct requires that true label. The tallest bar and the smiley face that appears after it cannot, on their own, show whether the network was right.

sections.title: Declare the layer sequence in PyTorch

teaching.text: The same vowel network can be written in **PyTorch**, a library for building neural networks. The code declares the network’s structure in a few lines.
The first lines load the tools.
children: **import torch** loads the PyTorch library.
**import torch.nn as nn** loads its neural-network module and gives it the short name **nn**.
The finished model is assigned to the variable **net**.

teaching.text: **nn.Sequential** builds the network as an ordered stack of layers.
children: Information passes through the layers in exactly the order they are listed.
A comment in the code records the shape as purely linear, **2 to 3 to 2 to 4 to 5**.
Each **nn.Linear** layer takes its incoming values and produces weighted sums from them.

teaching.text: The four layers match the picture of the network exactly.
children: **nn.Linear(2, 3, bias=False)** takes the 2 inputs to 3 outputs, the first hidden layer.
**nn.Linear(3, 2, bias=False)** takes those 3 values to 2.
**nn.Linear(2, 4, bias=False)** takes 2 values to 4.
**nn.Linear(4, 5, bias=False)** takes 4 values to the 5 outputs.
Each layer’s output count matches the next layer’s input count, which is what allows information to pass all the way through. The final five values correspond to the five candidate words.

teaching.text: **nn.Linear(in, out)** holds an **out × in weight matrix**, with one weight for every connection between the two layers.
children: The option **bias=False** removes the **bias**, an extra constant that a layer could otherwise add to each weighted sum.
Removing the bias does not remove any weights and does not prevent learning. It keeps every layer a **pure linear map**, matching the picture.

teaching.text: The code is a **declaration only, with no training**.
children: No activation layers appear anywhere in the sequence, so the whole network stays linear.
Declaring the structure does not train the network, and it does not compute the illustrated probability bars.
Training would require example inputs with their true labels, together with a process for changing the weights.

lecture15.title: Neural Networks · Forward propagation, learning, and sigmoid

sections.title: Neural Networks
Two formants feed a fully connected network

teaching.text: The vowel network is built to take in two formant measurements and give back a response for each of five words. Its two inputs are **F1** and **F2**, the first two formants of a recorded vowel. Its five outputs stand for **done, dune, dean, Don** and **Dan**, in that order from top to bottom.
children: The inputs carry measurements of the sound, numbers in hertz.
The outputs carry the network’s response to each possible word.
Both kinds of position are drawn as circles, but they play completely different roles in the network.

teaching.text: Between the inputs and outputs are three **hidden layers**.
children: The hidden layers contain **three, two and four** neurons.
The full arrangement is **2 to 3 to 2 to 4 to 5**. These numbers count the neurons in successive layers. They do not count recordings, words or training trials.
Each hidden neuron receives values from every neuron in the layer before it, combines them, and sends its result onward to every neuron in the next layer.

teaching.text: The network is **fully connected**, so every neuron in one layer connects to every neuron in the next.
children: Each connection has its own **weight**, a number that controls how the value traveling along that connection contributes to the receiving neuron.

All **40** illustrative signed weights are revealed together. They include very small values such as **+0.005** and **−0.001** on the connections from the formants, and larger ones such as **+0.6**, **−0.4** and **+0.8** deeper in the network.
A **positive weight** keeps the sign of its contribution, and a **negative weight** reverses it. The receiving neuron then combines all of its incoming contributions.

teaching.text: The same input can affect several neurons differently.
children: F1 reaches all three neurons of the first hidden layer, but through three different weights, so it is not multiplied by the same number on every connection.
F2 also reaches those same three neurons through its own three weights.
Each first-layer neuron therefore combines the same two measurements in its own particular way.

teaching.text: The weights stay fixed across both of these network pictures.
children: Changing a formant measurement changes what travels through the connections.
Changing a weight changes how strongly a connection contributes.
These are two different kinds of change to the system. A weight describes how one connection contributes to one neuron. It does not give the probability of any individual word.

sections.title: Forward propagation combines weighted inputs

teaching.text: **Forward propagation** is the process of carrying information from the inputs, through each hidden layer in turn, to the outputs. The example uses the input **F1 = 320** and **F2 = 2000**.
The top neuron of the first hidden layer computes **w₁ times F1 plus w₂ times F2**.
children: Its weight from F1 is **+0.005**, and its weight from F2 is **−0.001**.
F1 therefore contributes +0.005 times 320, a positive amount, and F2 contributes −0.001 times 2000, a negative amount.
Adding these two contributions gives **−0.40**. The negative contribution from F2 outweighs the positive contribution from F1.

teaching.text: This operation, multiplying each input by its weight and adding the products, is called an **inner product**.
children: The other two neurons of the first hidden layer receive the same two formants, but through their own weights, so their results are **6.64** and **2.72**.
A negative result such as −0.40 is still an ordinary value that the next layer can use. It does not mean the neuron has switched off or that its connections have disappeared.

teaching.text: Each later layer repeats exactly the same operation on the values from the layer immediately before it.
children: The second hidden layer produces approximately **5.50** and **−5.93**.
Those two values then produce the third hidden layer’s four values, approximately **1.57, −1.95, −1.95** and **−2.88**.
Information has to move in this order. Each neuron needs the finished results of the layer before it, so the layers are computed one after another.

teaching.text: The five final weighted sums are called **logits**, scores that are not yet probabilities.
children: **Softmax** turns them into probabilities. It raises e to the power of each logit and divides each result by the sum of all five, so the probabilities are positive and add up to exactly 1.
A negative logit therefore still becomes a positive probability, and a positive hidden value is not itself a probability.

teaching.text: **Done** receives the largest probability, about **55.7%**.
children: The others follow with **Don** at about 18.5%, **Dan** at about 10.2%, **dean** at about **8.1%** and **dune** at about 7.4%.
These are the network’s current responses to this one input. They do not establish which word was actually spoken.
The hidden activations here are linear, the weights stay fixed during the forward pass, and the calculations keep more precision than the rounded numbers displayed.

sections.title: Pop quiz · Forward propagation
Info on Exam 2 and Exam 3
Backpropagation uses the difference between prediction and target

teaching.text: **Backpropagation** is the method that tells the network how to change its weights. It begins by comparing two things, what the network produced and what it should have produced.
The **computed output** is the network’s current probability distribution.
children: For the example input, it gives **done** about **55.7%**, **Don** 18.5%, **Dan** 10.2%, **dean** only **8.1%** and **dune** 7.4%.

teaching.text: The **desired output** identifies the correct word.
children: It puts a **1** on **dean** and a **0** on each of the other four words, because dean is the word in this recording.

This target says which word belongs to the recording. It does not describe what the untrained network already produces, so the network’s largest response can disagree with the desired word, as it does here.

teaching.text: **Cross-entropy loss** measures how far the computed output is from the desired one.
children: It uses the probability that the network gives to the true word, so for this example the loss is the negative logarithm of the probability of dean.
Dean currently receives only about 8.1%, so the loss is large. Giving dean more probability lowers the loss, and giving it less raises the loss.

teaching.text: Backpropagation works **backward**, from the output connections toward the input connections.
children: The final layer’s contribution to the loss is found first, because those weights connect directly to the outputs.
That information is then used to find how hidden layer 3 contributed, then hidden layer 2 and finally hidden layer 1.
As each step finishes, the layer’s weights are replaced by updated values. For example, a weight of **+0.1** becomes **+0.083**, **−0.2** becomes **−0.202** and **+0.6** becomes **+0.622**.

teaching.text: A **gradient** describes how the loss changes when one weight changes by a small amount.
children: The **weight update** rule replaces each weight with the old weight minus the learning rate, **η**, times the gradient.
A positive gradient therefore decreases the weight, and a negative gradient increases it. Learning does not mean making every positive connection larger or every negative one smaller.

teaching.text: The activations and probabilities stored from the forward pass stay fixed throughout the backward calculation.
children: All of the gradients use the original weights and stored activations, so they belong to one simultaneous update, even though the updates are revealed layer by layer.
A new forward pass is needed to see the updated network’s predictions.
The input connections use a much smaller learning rate than the others, because their inputs are raw formant values in hertz, which are large numbers.

sections.title: Predict how changing a marked weight affects error

teaching.text: The question is direct. **If we increase this w, will the error go up or down?** Answering it means tracing what a small weight change does to the probability of the correct word.
children: The desired word is **dean**.
The network currently gives its largest probability to **done**, a wrong answer.
A weight change helps if it raises the probability of dean, and it hurts if it lowers it.

teaching.text: The **pink-marked** connection runs from the top neuron of the last hidden layer to the output for **done**.
children: It is a positive connection, and the hidden neuron that feeds it has a positive activation of about **1.57**.
Increasing this weight therefore raises the final score for done.
Softmax makes the five output probabilities share a single total of 1. Boosting the score of a wrong word takes probability away from the others, including dean.
So increasing this weight makes the cross-entropy loss go **up**, and the update should **decrease** it.

teaching.text: The **blue-marked** connection runs from **F1** to the top neuron of the first hidden layer.
children: Increasing this weight raises the value of that first hidden neuron, because F1 is a positive number.
From there, the change passes through several layers of positive and negative connections and eventually reaches all five outputs.
Some paths might raise dean’s score and others might lower it. Looking only at the sign of this first connection cannot decide which way the final error will move.

teaching.text: The full backward calculation answers the question for this network and the dean target.
children: The gradient for the blue input connection also comes out **positive**.
A small increase in this weight therefore raises the error, and the update **decreases** the weight.

In this example, both marked connections call for decreases. The late connection’s direction can be read almost directly from the output, while the early connection’s direction required combining the influence of every downstream path, which is exactly the work backpropagation does.

sections.title: Backpropagation reuses downstream error calculations

teaching.text: Why do neural networks **backpropagate**, working from the output back toward the input? The answer comes from comparing the problem of changing the **last** set of weights with the problem of changing the **first** set.
Consider the **last weights, W5**, which connect the final hidden layer to the outputs.
children: The output probabilities are **directly determined** by these weights.
The error is therefore very directly determined by them as well.
Once the computed and desired outputs are known, their difference can be used right away to work out better values for W5. No further layers stand in the way.

teaching.text: Now consider the **first weights, W2**, which connect the inputs to the first hidden layer.
children: W2 affects the first layer of activations.
Those activations affect another two layers of activations, along with all of the other weights in between, before the output is produced.
It is really hard to figure out the culpability of W2, how much it is to blame, for mistakes made all the way at the end.
Moreover, the effect of W2 on the errors **includes** the effect of W5, since W5 is downstream of W2. Whatever W2 changes must pass through W5 to reach the output.

teaching.text: So which problem is easier, improving W2 or improving W5?
children: **W5 is easy.**
Improving W2 depends on knowing what the later layers do, so its problem contains W5’s problem inside it.
The natural strategy is to solve the small problems first and then use their answers for the bigger problems that depend on them.

teaching.text: That strategy is called **dynamic programming**.
children: **Backpropagation is Bellman–Viterbi dynamic programming.**

It computes the effects of the weights nearest the output first and stores them. When it reaches an earlier layer, it reuses those stored results instead of redoing the entire downstream calculation separately for every early weight.
Working backward fits the structure of the problem, because the effect of each early layer includes all the layers after it.

teaching.text: In short, **backpropagation = SGD + dynamic programming**.
children: **SGD**, stochastic gradient descent, is the rule that adjusts each weight a little in the direction that reduces the error.
Backpropagation supplies the gradients that SGD needs, and dynamic programming is what makes computing those gradients efficient.

sections.title: Pair each recording with its target row

teaching.text: Training a network requires examples together with their correct answers. These are stored in two **training matrices**, one for inputs and one for targets, and the network diagram beside them still shows the activations from before backpropagation.
The **Formant_Inputs** matrix is **110 × 2**, meaning 110 rows and 2 columns.
children: Each row holds **F1** and **F2** for one recording, in hertz.
The two columns are the two sound measurements, not two possible words.
The network processes the two values in one row together, as a single example.

teaching.text: The **TrueVowel_Outputs** matrix is **110 × 5**.
children: Its five columns, in order, are **done, dune, dean, Don** and **Dan**.
For each recording, the row puts a **1** in the column of the correct word and a **0** in each of the other four.
This kind of target is called **one-hot**, because exactly one position is switched on to identify the category.

teaching.text: The illustrative rows show how measurements pair with words.
children: The formants **500 and 1500** pair with **done**.
**350 and 1000** pair with **dune**.
**320 and 2000** pair with **dean**. This third row is the very example that has been run through the network.
**700 and 1100** pair with **Don**, and **800 and 1700** pair with **Dan**.
These five rows are teaching examples that show the column layout. They are not the full dataset.

teaching.text: The rows of the two matrices must stay matched exactly.
children: The third input row, 320 and 2000, belongs with the third target row, which identifies dean.
If an input row were moved without moving its matching target row, the sound measurements would be paired with the wrong answer.
Having the same number of rows is not enough, because the order must also agree. The full matrices contain 110 examples, each a paired row.
The five target columns list the possible categories. They do not mean that each recording supplies five separate examples.

teaching.text: The network’s current output is a separate thing from the target matrix.
children: Before backpropagation, the network gives its own probabilities to the five words, with **done** highest, at 55.7%, for the dean example.
The target records the correct label even while the network is making a mistake.
Training works by comparing these two kinds of information. It never replaces the target with the network’s strongest response.

sections.title: Read one full-batch training step in PyTorch

teaching.text: A complete training step for the vowel network can be written as a short **PyTorch** program. It performs one gradient step using all 110 recordings at once, which is called a **full-batch** step.
The program begins by loading the data.
children: **import torch** and **from torch import nn** load the library and its neural-network tools.
**X = torch.load("Formant_Inputs.pt").float()** loads the formant matrix, which is **110 × 2**.
**Y = torch.load("TrueVowel_Outputs.pt").float()** loads the target matrix, which is **110 × 5**.
**.float()** makes sure both are floating-point tensors. The program assumes these files have already been saved with torch.save. It does not create the recordings or their labels.

teaching.text: The network is declared with **nn.Sequential**, which connects its layers in the order they are written.
children: **nn.Linear(2, 3)** maps each pair of inputs to three values.
**nn.Linear(3, 2)**, **nn.Linear(2, 4)** and **nn.Linear(4, 5)** follow, keeping the **2 to 3 to 2 to 4 to 5** arrangement.
No activation function such as sigmoid is declared between these layers.

teaching.text: The final five lines perform the training step itself.
children: **sgd = torch.optim.SGD(net.parameters(), lr=0.1)** sets up stochastic gradient descent, giving it the network’s parameters and a **learning rate of 0.1**.
**sgd.zero_grad()** clears any gradients stored from before.

**loss = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()(net(X), Y)** runs the forward pass on all of X and compares the resulting scores with Y. CrossEntropyLoss performs the softmax-related calculation internally, so the final linear layer supplies logits rather than a separately declared softmax output.
**loss.backward()** computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every parameter.
**sgd.step()** changes the parameters using those gradients.

teaching.text: These operations each do a separate job.
children: Computing how a weight affects the error does not change that weight by itself. Only the step does that.
Clearing gradients does not erase the learned parameter values.

teaching.text: All **110 rows** contribute to this single gradient step, and the code has no loop that repeats training.
children: The program uses PyTorch’s default starting weights and default bias settings, while the drawn network uses hand-selected weights with no biases.
The code specifies the same layer sizes as the drawing, but it does not automatically reproduce the drawing’s numbers.

sections.title: Sigmoid turns an inner product into a bounded activation

teaching.text: The **sigmoid activation function** is written **σ(z) = 1 / (1 + exp(−z))**. It takes an inner product, z, as its input and returns a value between 0 and 1. Adding it to a network changes how each neuron responds to its weighted sum.
The sigmoid squashes extreme values toward its two limits.
children: If the inner product is **large and positive**, the sigmoid is **near 1**.
If the inner product is **large and negative**, the sigmoid is **basically 0**.
For an inner product of **−4**, **σ(−4) = 0.0180**. For an inner product of **4**, **σ(4) = 0.9820**.

teaching.text: The function traces an S-shaped curve.
children: The horizontal axis is the **linear activation**, the weighted sum before sigmoid is applied.
The vertical axis is the **sigmoid activation**, the value after sigmoid is applied.
The curve is steep around the middle and flattens out near both the top and the bottom. Near the flat ends, further changes in the input produce only small changes in the output.
The change is gradual rather than an exact switch between two values.

teaching.text: The formula explains this shape.
children: When z is large and positive, exp(−z) becomes tiny, so the denominator approaches 1 and the output approaches 1.
When z is large and negative, exp(−z) becomes huge, so the denominator grows and the output approaches 0.

teaching.text: **Lord Edgar Adrian**, who received the **Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1932**, supplies the biological motivation.
children: In his account, **neurons are nearly digital**, on or off, roughly.

Adrian’s work concerned how often nerve fibers fire, so the sigmoid is a model of graded activation that behaves almost like a switch at its extremes. It is not a claim that real neurons have only two possible firing rates.

teaching.text: **Animal perception** reflects this kind of response.
children: Some things that seem alike are perceived as different, and some things that are very different are perceived as the same.

The sigmoid behaves the same way. Two inputs on opposite sides of the steep middle can produce very different outputs, while two quite different inputs near one flat end produce almost the same output. Similar incoming measurements do not always produce similar responses.

sections.title: Apply sigmoid while recalculating downstream activity

teaching.text: To see what sigmoid does, it is applied to the network **one neuron at a time**. The inputs stay **F1 = 320** and **F2 = 2000**, and the connection weights never change.
children: **Purple** neurons still use a linear activation, passing their inner product along unchanged.
**Green** neurons pass their inner product through sigmoid.
The nine hidden neurons are switched over in layer order, the three of the first hidden layer, then the two of the second, then the four of the third.

teaching.text: The first switch changes the top neuron of the first hidden layer from **−0.400** to about **0.401**.
children: That new output changes what every neuron in the next layer receives.
So all of the downstream values are **recalculated**, all the way to the outputs.

This builds a genuine sigmoid network step by step. It is not the same as wrapping sigmoid around each number stored from the all-linear network, because once an earlier output changes, every later weighted sum changes too.

teaching.text: After all three first-layer neurons use sigmoid, their outputs are about **0.401, 0.999** and **0.938**.
children: The second layer’s weighted sums are recalculated from those values and then passed through sigmoid, giving about **0.713** and **0.223**.
Those values feed the third layer, whose final sigmoid outputs are about **0.599, 0.609, 0.609** and **0.481**.

teaching.text: The output layer still uses **softmax** to assign probabilities across the five words.
children: Once every hidden neuron uses sigmoid, **Dan** has the largest probability, about **32.0%**.
**Dean** has about **23.0%**, **dune** about 20.2%, **done** about 16.2% and **Don** about 8.5%.
The relative pattern of outputs has changed dramatically, even though the inputs and the connection weights are exactly the same as before.

teaching.text: This sequence changes the activation rule. It does not train the weights.
children: Dean’s probability is much higher than its 8.1% in the all-linear network, but dean is still not the largest response.
Adding sigmoid can therefore change which word the network favors without showing that the network has learned the correct classification. Learning still requires backpropagation and weight updates.

sections.title: Insert sigmoid after the hidden linear layers

teaching.text: The PyTorch program for the sigmoid network is the same as the earlier one, with **sigmoid** activations inserted after the hidden layers.
The data loading is unchanged.
children: **X** is loaded from Formant_Inputs.pt as a **110 × 2** matrix of formants.
**Y** is loaded from TrueVowel_Outputs.pt as a **110 × 5** matrix of one-hot targets.

teaching.text: The network declaration now includes **nn.Sigmoid()** three times.
children: It follows **nn.Linear(2, 3)**, **nn.Linear(3, 2)** and **nn.Linear(2, 4)**.
Each hidden layer therefore first combines its incoming values into weighted sums and then transforms those sums with sigmoid before passing them on.
The network still receives **two formant measurements** and still produces **five output scores**.

teaching.text: Sigmoid changes the values without changing how many there are.
children: The three values from the first linear layer are still three values after sigmoid, so **nn.Linear(3, 2)** still receives exactly the input size it expects.
The same holds after the two-value and four-value hidden layers.
The layer dimensions stay **2 to 3 to 2 to 4 to 5**.

teaching.text: The final layer, **nn.Linear(4, 5)**, is not followed by a sigmoid.
children: Its five scores are logits that go to **CrossEntropyLoss**, which performs the softmax-related calculation internally.
Hidden sigmoid activations and the final class-probability calculation have different jobs. Adding a hidden activation does not turn any hidden neuron into one of the five word categories.

teaching.text: The training sequence is the same as before.
children: **sgd.zero_grad()** clears the old gradients.
The forward pass and **CrossEntropyLoss** compare the predictions with the paired targets.
**loss.backward()** computes the parameter gradients, and **sgd.step()** applies the update.
The learning rate is still **0.1**, and all 110 recordings contribute to the one step shown.

teaching.text: The drawn network and the code differ in one important way.
children: The drawing uses the original illustrative weights with no biases, which gives Dan about **32.0%** and dean about **23.0%** once sigmoid is added.
The short PyTorch declaration starts with its own default weights and bias options.
Its structure matches the drawing’s change in hidden activation, but reproducing the drawing’s exact probabilities would also require the matching weights and bias choices.
